title: Co-existent autoimmune diseases in people with multiple sclerosis and a review on choice of immunotherapy.
abstract: Coexisting autoimmune diseases in multiple sclerosis (MS) may influence disease-modifying therapy (DMT) choice, but Indian data remains limited. This study aims to determine the prevalence of co-existent autoimmune disorders in Indian MS patients and assess their impact on DMT selection. This multicentre, cross-sectional observational study included 355 adults with MS evaluated across five Indian neuroimmunology clinics between 2016 and 2026. Comorbidity prevalence was compared against general-population estimates, and DMT utilization was compared between patients with and without autoimmune comorbidities. Fifty-nine patients (16.6%) had an autoimmune disorder, with hypothyroidism (5.9%), rheumatoid arthritis (RA; 2.0%), and type 1 diabetes mellitus (1.4%) being the most common. Prevalences of RA (2.0% vs 0.49%; Autoimmune comorbidity occurred in about 1/6 Indian MS patients, with excess RA and IBD relative to population prevalence and an associated shift in DMT selection.

title: Revisiting Daclizumab for Multiple Sclerosis: A Systematic Evaluation of a Targeted Immunotherapy.
abstract: Daclizumab is a humanized monoclonal antibody that blocks the interleukin-2 receptor α-chain (CD25) and reduces activation of auto reactive T cells. It attenuates disease activity by reducing gadolinium-enhancing lesions in patients with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (MS). Therefore, this systematic review aimed to revisit the therapeutic role of Daclizumab in MS patients with a particular focus on immune system parameters and its adverse events. This systematic literature review included all published clinical trials from 2000 to 2025 regardless of publication date or language, identified through searches of Embase, Medline, Cochrane, Scopus, and other databases. Daclizumab reduced the relapse frequency and disease activity; however, it was associated with serious safety concerns. The common complication in most patients with multiple sclerosis was hepatotoxicity and elevated liver enzymes. Furthermore, the cutaneous side effects occurred in 19-34% of patients, from mild rashes to serious dermatologic disorders such as psoriasis. Also, it was associated with an increased rate of upper respiratory infections in multiple sclerosis patients. Daclizumab therapy also promoted the expansion of CD56^bright^ natural killer (NK) cells and reduced the number of CD4+ T cells and CD25+ Foxp3- T regulatory cells. These findings suggest that Daclizumab may demonstrate promising treatment effects in MS patients by affecting the IL-2 receptor signaling pathway, modulating lymphocyte activity, and improving MS symptoms. However, because of documented complications, more research strategies are needed, and current treatment protocols should be revised.

title: Factor Structure and Psychometric Properties of the Intolerance of Uncertainty Scale-12 in Multiple Sclerosis.
abstract: Despite the high prevalence of anxiety disorders in multiple sclerosis (MS) and the inherent uncertainty associated with the disease, it is unclear whether current measures of intolerance of uncertainty (IU) are appropriate for people with MS. In this study, we describe the psychometric features of the short-form Intolerance of Uncertainty Scale (IUS-12) in a mixed sample of 2,084 participants (244 MS, 1,840 non-MS controls). A bifactor model best represented the IUS-12 in the MS group. The IUS-12 appeared suitable in MS, demonstrating good construct validity and moderate test-retest reliability over the 6-month survey period. Measurement invariance was found across MS and non-MS participants. Of note, IU scores were comparable between groups, but IU showed stronger associations with anxiety-related pathologies in participants with MS than non-MS controls. Routine assessment incorporating the IUS-12 may help clarify factors underpinning anxiety and inform the development of targeted psychological interventions for people with MS.

title: Depression, adverse childhood experiences, and cigarette smoking are associated with suicide attempts in people with multiple sclerosis: a cross-sectional exploratory study.
abstract: People with multiple sclerosis (pwMS) are at elevated risk of suicide compared to the general population. This exploratory study aimed to identify clinical factors associated with suicide attempts in pwMS, which is crucial for developing tailored suicide prevention strategies. In a cross-sectional retrospective sample of pwMS consecutively assessed at a Toronto-based neuropsychiatry clinic between July 2024 and January 2026, data were gathered about demographics, disease-related factors, and psychiatric clinical factors. Participants were asked about any prior suicide attempts (coded as presence or absence) as part of routine care. Candidate explanatory variables of prior suicide attempts were identified with t-tests and chi-square analyses (p < 0.10). A backward stepwise logistic regression analysis was undertaken to estimate the odds of any prior suicide attempts from candidate variables (p < 0.05). In 360 pwMS, mean age was 46.1 years (SD = 13.1), 69.7% were female, median Expanded Disability Status Scale score was 2.5 (IQR = 1.5-5.0), and 8.6% had attempted suicide. Candidate variables were parenthood status (p = 0.030), adverse childhood experiences (p = 0.004), illness subtype (p = 0.049), cigarette use (p = 0.003), depression (p < 0.001), post-traumatic stress disorder (p < 0.001), suicidal ideation (p < 0.001), and age (p = 0.059). In the final model, depression (OR = 2.6, 95% CI [1.1, 6.1], p = 0.029), cigarette use (OR = 3.2, 95% CI [1.2,8.2], p = 0.017), and adverse childhood experiences (OR = 2.8, 95% CI [1.2,6.7], p = 0.019) were linked to increased odds of suicide attempts. Parenthood was associated with decreased odds of suicide attempts (OR = 0.3, 95%CI [0.1, 0.8], p = 0.017). In summary, among pwMS, those with depression, who smoke cigarettes, and who report adverse childhood experiences are more likely to have attempted suicide, while parenthood may be protective.

title: Nervous System-Specific SARM1 Knockout Attenuates Optic Neuritis in a Multiple Sclerosis Mouse Model.
abstract: In optic neuritis, a complication of multiple sclerosis (MS), the main pathological manifestations are autoimmune-mediated inflammatory infiltration, myelin loss, and axonal damage. We generated conditional SARM1 cKO mice in the nervous system and performed MOG

title: Biobehavioral correlates of perceived health-related quality of life in relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis: Toward an extended framework for understanding health impact.
abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an immune-mediated central nervous system disorder; relapsing-remitting MS (RRMS) is the most common form. Self-perceived health-related quality of life (HRQoL) has been linked to psycho-behavioral and immunological factors, but their interplay remains unclear. We examined psycho-behavioral, clinical, and immunological correlates of perceived physical and mental health. In this cross-sectional study, 85 patients with RRMS (78% female; mean age 40.6 ± 10.3 years; predominantly mild disability) were assessed for fatigue, sleep quality, daytime sleepiness, anxiety/depression symptoms, and perceived cognitive dysfunction. Blood samples were analyzed for complete blood counts and, in a subgroup, lymphocyte subpopulations; the systemic immune-inflammation index (SII) was calculated. HRQoL was measured using the SF-36 Physical and Mental Component Summaries (PCS and MCS). Hierarchical linear regression models included sociodemographic, clinical, and treatment-class covariates, with sensitivity analyses. Disability, fatigue, and depressive symptoms were associated with lower PCS, and sleep disturbances and depressive symptoms with lower MCS. Higher lymphocyte count was associated with higher MCS (β = +0.268, p = 0.006; ΔR HRQoL in RRMS showed psychological and clinical associations, with an additional lymphocyte-MCS association. The clinical relevance of the immune findings, including the exploratory NK-PCS association, requires further investigation.

title: Phytocannabinoids in neurologic, neuropsychiatric, inflammatory, pain, cardiometabolic, hepatic, renal, and neoplastic disorders: Pharmacology, clinical evidence, and translational perspectives.
abstract: Phytocannabinoids are pharmacologically diverse constituents of Cannabis sativa whose actions go beyond canonical cannabinoid receptors. Δ9-Tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) and cannabidiol (CBD) are best characterized, while cannabigerol, cannabidivarin, tetrahydrocannabivarin, cannabichromene, cannabinol, and related compounds are emerging candidates. This review integrates molecular pharmacology, pharmacokinetics, safety, and therapeutic evidence across neurologic, neuropsychiatric, inflammatory, pain, cardiovascular and metabolic, hepatic, renal, and neoplastic disorders. The strongest evidence supports pharmaceutical-grade oral CBD as adjunctive therapy for seizures associated with Dravet syndrome, Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, and tuberous sclerosis complex, and standardized THC-CBD formulations for selected patients with multiple sclerosis-associated spasticity. Emerging clinical signals in schizophrenia, pain, fibromyalgia, sleep disturbance, substance-use disorders, dermatologic conditions, sickle cell disease, and other symptom-focused indications support continued development. However, efficacy remains compound-, formulation-, exposure-, and indication-specific. In oncology, supportive-care applications must remain distinct from tumor-directed treatment, for which clinical efficacy has not been established. Preclinical studies show coherent effects on neuronal excitability, glial and immune activation, endothelial dysfunction, oxidative and nitrative stress, mitochondrial injury, fibrosis, and regulated cell death. These findings support further investigation in neurodegeneration, ischemia-reperfusion injury, diabetic cardiovascular disease, immune-mediated disorders, hepatic and renal injury, and selected cancers. Translation is constrained by product heterogeneity, variable exposure, uncertain target engagement, model differences, drug interactions, and underpowered trials. Standardized products, exposure-informed dosing, pharmacodynamic biomarkers, responder-enriched designs, and indication-specific randomized studies can address these barriers. Phytocannabinoids therefore represent a promising therapeutic platform whose potential will be best realized by matching defined compounds and formulations to biologically coherent diseases, mechanisms, treatment windows, and patient populations.

title: Propionate, a short-chain fatty acid, is associated with disease activity in pediatric-onset multiple sclerosis.
authors: US Network of Pediatric MS Centers
abstract: Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), metabolites found in fermented foods and produced by colonic bacterial fermentation of dietary fibers, may mediate gut-brain axis crosstalk influencing the course of multiple sclerosis (MS). In this study, SCFAs are measured in plasma and paired stool samples by targeted mass spectrometry in a large cohort of deeply phenotyped individuals shortly after MS onset. Propionate is consistently associated with a protective effect on three clinical and imaging activity-related outcomes. Findings are reproduced in an equally large external cohort for plasma and stool measurements. Despite the correlation between plasma SCFAs and SCFA-producing gut microbial taxa, propionate levels are not correlated with dietary fiber, suggesting that intake may not be sufficient to modulate its levels and ensuing inflammation. In conclusion, propionate is consistently associated with lower disease activity, and exogenous administration may be more likely than fiber supplementation to confer protective effects on MS activity in proof-of-concept clinical trials.

title: Neurobehavioral phenotypes in multiple sclerosis: a data-driven classification using latent profile analysis.
journal: Neurological sciences : official journal of the Italian Neurological Society and of the Italian Society of Clinical Neurophysiology
abstract: Cognitive impairment in multiple sclerosis (MS) is highly heterogeneous. Emerging evidence suggests that patients may cluster into distinct cognitive and affective phenotypes. Characterizing these phenotypes using clinically feasible tools is essential for improving stratification, prognostication, and the development of targeted monitoring and intervention strategies in routine MS care. To identify neurobehavioral phenotypes in people with MS using a clinically feasible assessment battery and to evaluate the classification accuracy of individual measures for phenotype classification. In this single-center cross-sectional study, 837 patients underwent clinical and neuropsychological assessments. Cognitive performance was evaluated using the Brief International Cognitive Assessment for Multiple Sclerosis (BICAMS). Depressive symptoms and levels of fatigue were also assessed. Latent profile analysis was performed. Post hoc analyses examined demographic and clinical differences between phenotypes. Receiver operating characteristic analyses assessed the ability of individual measures to discriminate among phenotypes. The identified phenotypes were: Neuropsychologically Preserved (NP; 58.0%), mild Global Cognitive Dysfunction-Visuospatial Memory Predominant (mGCD-Vsp; 24.1%), significant Global Cognitive Dysfunction-Depression (sGCD-Depression; 5.1%), and Isolated Depression (I-Depression; 12.8%). More impaired phenotypes were associated with older age, longer disease duration, greater disability, progressive disease courses, and more frequent use of high-efficacy disease-modifying therapies. Visuospatial memory test demonstrated the highest discriminative accuracy for the mGCD-Vsp phenotype, whereas depression scores most accurately identified the sGCD-Depression and I-Depression phenotypes. Distinct neurobehavioral phenotypes were identified in MS using brief cognitive and affective assessments routinely employed in clinical practice. The provision of classification accuracy metrics may facilitate clinical implementation and personalized monitoring and rehabilitation.

title: Association of comorbid migraine with fatigue and health-related quality of life in multiple sclerosis: A cross-sectional study.
journal: Neurological sciences : official journal of the Italian Neurological Society and of the Italian Society of Clinical Neurophysiology
abstract: Migraine is a common comorbidity in multiple sclerosis (MS) and may increase symptom burden. Evidence from non-Western MS populations remains limited, especially regarding its association with fatigue and health-related quality of life (HRQoL). This study examined the clinical correlates of comorbid migraine in patients with MS. This cross-sectional study recruited 296 adult patients with MS from a tertiary care center. Migraine was diagnosed according to ICHD-3 criteria. Fatigue severity was measured with the Fatigue Severity Scale (FSS), while HRQoL was assessed with the Arabic Short Form-36. Comorbid migraine was present in 81 patients (27.4%). Female sex was associated with higher odds of comorbid migraine (adjusted OR = 3.35, 95% CI 1.46-7.7, p = 0.004). Current interferon use was also associated with higher odds of comorbid migraine compared with other DMTs (adjusted OR = 3.70, 95% CI 1.09-12.56, p = 0.036). Patients with migraine had more frequent fatigue (78% vs. 64%, p = 0.026), higher FSS scores (median 4.78 vs. 4.22, p = 0.002), and lower MCS scores (median 39 vs. 50, p < 0.001). PCS did not differ significantly in the unadjusted comparison (p = 0.18). In adjusted models, migraine was also associated with lower MCS (p < 0.001) and higher FSS score (p = 0.015). Comorbid migraine was common among patients with MS and was associated with higher fatigue burden and lower mental HRQoL. These findings support migraine as a clinically relevant comorbidity in MS and highlight the importance of systematic evaluation and coordinated care in patients reporting migraine and related symptom burden.

title: Understanding discourses on multiple sclerosis medications and side effects in an online support group: a Latent Dirichlet Allocation analysis.
abstract: Understanding how individuals discuss medication side effects in online support communities is critical for informing patient-centred care and addressing misinformation in chronic illness contexts. This study examines discourse surrounding multiple sclerosis (MS) treatments and side effects in an online support group for people living with MS. A corpus of approximately 112,000 words comprising discussions of medications and their associated side effects was analysed using Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), supplemented by thematic analysis, to identify dominant themes. A subsequent chi-square analysis examined differences in the distribution of themes across four treatment categories. Three interrelated themes were identified in the corpus: (1) treatment use, administration, and risk considerations, (2) illness experiences, treatment evaluations, and comparisons, and (3) symptom burden and clinical monitoring. Among these, illness experiences, treatment evaluations, and comparisons emerged as the most prevalent theme, highlighting the centrality of lived experience and emotional expression in online discourse. Statistical analysis revealed a significant association between theme distribution and treatment category, χ²(6) = 142.45, p < .001, with a moderate effect size (Cramér's V = 0.29). The findings demonstrate that discussions of MS treatments and side effects in online support communities extend beyond biomedical concerns and are closely tied to experiential, emotional, and symptom-related dimensions of illness management. Online communities therefore function as important spaces for information exchange, experiential sharing, and treatment evaluation. The study shows the need to integrate patient perspectives and experiential concerns into clinical communication, particularly regarding treatment expectations and side effects. The findings also underline the importance of strengthening digital health literacy and pharmacovigilance efforts to improve the quality of treatment-related information available in online support communities.

title: The preclinical efficacy of Panax ginseng in multiple sclerosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis with a perspective on clinical translation.
abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic autoimmune neurodegenerative disorder with limited disease-modifying therapies. We searched MEDLINE, ScienceDirect, Scopus, Web of Science, and Cochrane CENTRAL through October 2025. Standardized mean differences (SMD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated using random-effects models. Primary outcomes were disease severity and central nervous system (CNS) histopathology in animal models, and fatigue scores in clinical trials. Ten preclinical and two clinical studies met inclusion criteria. In animal models,

title: CAR T cells show early promise in progressive multiple sclerosis.
Feasibility of applying generative AI to create managed care pharmacy formulary reviews.
journal: American journal of health-system pharmacy : AJHP : official journal of the American Society of Health-System Pharmacists
abstract: Formulary reviews are used with other data sources and clinical judgement to support formulary strategies, such as placement for existing and new-to-market drugs. We describe the pharmacy resident user experience and assessed the feasibility of using clinical and research-focused generative artificial (genAI) tools in a managed care setting for creating formulary reviews for 2 complex and rare diseases: multiple sclerosis and age-related macular degeneration. This allowed genAI feasibility assessment for disease states with less well-defined guidelines and fewer data sources from which to draw information. Users reported a steeper learning curve with research-specific genAI systems compared with pharmacy-focused tools. Users noted pharmacy-focused genAI tools may produce more current drug pipeline information, relative to research-focused AI systems. Prompt engineering, the skill of creating effective prompts to elicit accurate information from genAI models, also contributed to the quality of the evidence produced, regardless of the tool used. The pharmacists noted time savings when utilizing AI compared with a completely manual data generation process involving individual searches of PubMed, business reports, FDA websites, and pharmaceutical company-related information sources. Pharmacists need adequate time and training to optimize prompt techniques to produce quality health- and medication-related information and must be educated on potential downsides of genAI such as inaccurate or incomplete results. With currently available tools, all generated output required careful human fact checking. With continued use and accumulating experience, the pharmacist may become more efficient over time with genAI support for formulary reviews.

title: Treating Depression in Multiple Sclerosis with Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation: A Pilot Study.
journal: The Canadian journal of neurological sciences. Le journal canadien des sciences neurologiques
abstract: Depression is two to three times more common in people with multiple sclerosis (pwMS) than the general population. To evaluate the efficacy and tolerability of intermittent theta burst stimulation (iTBS) in treating depressive symptoms in pwMS and major depressive disorder (MDD). Twenty-one pwMS and MDD participated in an open-label 4-week trial of iTBS to the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (L-DLPFC). The Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HAMD-17), California Verbal Learning Test Second Edition Total Learning (CVLT-II-TL), Brief Visuospatial Memory Test - Revised Total Learning (BVMT-R-TL) and Symbol Digit Modalities Test (SDMT) were administered before and after treatment. The primary outcome was response rates on HAMD-17, defined as a >50% reduction from baseline. Depression scores decreased from baseline to post-treatment with a mean reduction of 10.24 points (d = 1.55, 95% CI 0.83 to 2.25, P < .001). Ten (58.8%) pwMS responded to treatment, and seven (41.2%) were non-responders (n = 17). The treatment response group showed lower depression scores post-treatment than non-responders (d = -3.01, 95% CI -4.43 to -1.55, P < .001). Post-treatment, responders showed higher visuospatial memory (d = 1.11, 95% CI 0.06 to 2.14, P = .039) and information processing scores (d = 1.74, 95% CI 0.58 to 2.87, P = .003) compared to non-responders. There were two drop-outs, and two participants were lost to follow-up. There were no serious adverse events. iTBS can improve depressive symptoms in pwMS and MDD and may be associated with cognitive improvement. NCT04621708.

title: Healthcare professionals' perceptions and experiences of promoting physical activity in persons with multiple sclerosis: a systematic review of qualitative evidence.
abstract: To synthesise existing evidence on healthcare professionals' perceptions and experiences of physical activity promotion in persons with multiple sclerosis (MS). The PRISMA and ENTREQ guidelines were used. SCOPUS, CINAHL, PubMed, Embase, PsycINFO and Web of Science databases were searched from database inception to 19 September 2025 to identify eligible studies. Search was limited to peer-reviewed articles, with a focus on healthcare professionals' views about physical activity promotion in persons with MS. Data were extracted and thematically analysed, and identified themes were synthesised. Eight studies met the selection criteria. Identified themes were related to health professional-based factors (knowledge of MS and awareness of physical activity types and benefits, skills, training and education, continuity of support and professional role), organisational factors (coordinated teamwork and proactive approach, policies, protocols and guidelines, availability and accessibility of physical activity opportunities), perceived social factors (social support networks) and perceived patient-related factors (MS-related symptoms, self-efficacy and motivation, limited knowledge and misconceptions, and financial limitations). Findings suggest that improving physical activity promotion in MS care requires MS-specific education and training for healthcare professionals, practical resources such as patient education materials and referral pathways, and stronger cross-sector coordination to sustain consistent practice.

title: Capability-Opportunity-Motivation-Behavior (COM-B) Correlates of Physical Activity in People with Multiple Sclerosis Who Have Analogue Generalized Anxiety Disorder.
abstract: Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) is prevalent, yet poorly managed among people with multiple sclerosis (MS). Physical activity (PA) may be a potential lifestyle, behavioral approach for managing GAD in MS. As a foundational step in developing PA behavior change interventions, this study applied the Capability-Opportunity-Motivation-Behavior (COM-B) model for explaining PA behavior in people with MS who have analogue GAD (AGAD). Participants (N = 320) prescreened for AGAD completed online surveys regarding PA (Godin Leisure Time Exercise Questionnaire (GLTEQ), Physical Activity Staging Questionnaire (PASQ)) and COM-B constructs. Participants were categorized into current PA groups based on GLTEQ scores, and long-term PA groups based on PASQ scores. Multivariate analysis of variance and discriminant function analysis (DFA) identified COM-B constructs that differentiated PA groups. All COM-B constructs significantly differed among current and long-term PA groups. DFA identified Action Control, Intention, Self-efficacies (Action, Maintenance, Recovery), Action and Coping Planning, and Goal Setting as primary constructs differentiating PA groups. This study identified factors within the Capability and Motivation domains of the COM-B model as primary correlates of PA in persons with MS and AGAD. Such results might guide the development of behavior change interventions for increasing PA and perhaps treating GAD in MS.

title: Pelvic neurology meets multiple sclerosis.
Four-Year Cognitive Outcomes in Multiple Sclerosis: Associations With Lesion Myelin Integrity.
journal: Annals of clinical and translational neurology
abstract: Cognitive impairment is prevalent in patients with multiple sclerosis (MS) but whether lesion myelin integrity influences future cognitive outcomes remains unclear. We investigated the relationship between baseline lesion myelin water fraction (MWF) and cognitive performance 4 years later. We conducted a longitudinal study of 118 patients with MS. Cognitive function was evaluated annually for 5 years using the symbol digit modalities test (SDMT), California verbal learning test-II (CVLT-II) immediate recall, and brief visuospatial memory test-revised (BVMT-R). Lesion level MWF maps were the primary variable of interest, while paramagnetic rim lesions (PRLs) and structural imaging measures were included as covariates. We used a functional linear regression model with both scalar and functional covariates, followed by a stepwise variable selection procedure. After adjustment for baseline cognition and clinical covariates, participants with higher baseline lesion-level MWF values in the mid-range of the lesion distribution exhibited better SDMT at 4 years (p = 0.006). Greater heterogeneity in lesion-level MWF was associated with worse visuospatial memory performance on the BVMT-R at Year 4. Conversely, lesion MWF was not associated with CVLT-II performance. Additional covariates in the final models included PRLs and cortical thinning for SDMT, PRLs and disease duration for BVMT-R, and thalamic atrophy for CVLT-II. Lesion myelin integrity was associated with future cognitive performance, particularly in domains of processing speed and visuospatial memory. These findings suggest that lesion demyelination contributes to cognitive outcomes in MS, which may provide a potential focus for future work improving risk stratification for cognitive impairment.

title: Yellow fever vaccination in multiple sclerosis: A retrospective single-centre case series.
abstract: To describe the clinical outcomes and safety of yellow fever vaccination (YFV) in patients with multiple sclerosis (MS) and the management of YFV according to the different disease modifying therapies (DMTs) around vaccination. Single-center retrospective observational study conducted at the Pitié-Salpêtrière hospital, Paris. All patients who followed for a central nervous system demyelinating disease and who received YFV between 2019 and 2024 were included. Twenty-six patients were included: 25 with MS and one with MOG-antibody-associated disease (MOGAD). Median age at vaccination was 34.5 years (range 22-58), and 21/26 (80.8%) were women. Two patients with relapsing-remitting MS experienced a clinical relapse within six months after YFV; both also had radiological activity. Brain MRI within six months after vaccination was available for only 8 patients; therefore the remaining patients could not be classified as free of radiological activity. Travel was the main reason for vaccination in 24/26 patients (92.3%): 17/26 (65.4%) had already planned a travel and 7/26 (26.9%) were vaccinated in anticipation of future travel, before the introduction of an immunosuppressive therapy. In the remaining 2 patients, YFV was a catch-up vaccination before the introduction of an immunosuppressive drug. No serious adverse event was documented in the medical records. No unexpected safety signal was identified in this small retrospective cohort pf patients with MS. Two relapses occurred after YFV in patients with potential confounding factors, including treatment interruption, MS activity before YFV and the postpartum period.

title: Artificial intelligence-based voice biomarkers for early detection and monitoring of neurological diseases: current evidence, limitations, and clinical perspectives.
abstract: Early diagnosis and longitudinal monitoring of neurological diseases remain major clinical challenges because current diagnostic approaches are often expensive, invasive, or insufficiently sensitive to detect early functional changes. In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising approach for analyzing voice and speech as non-invasive digital biomarkers capable of capturing subtle alterations associated with neurological dysfunction. This narrative review analyzed studies published between 2015 and 2026 retrieved from PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar. The review critically examines the limitations of current neurological diagnostic methods, summarizes the available evidence on AI-based voice and speech biomarkers, discusses machine learning and deep learning approaches applied to speech analysis, and evaluates the methodological, ethical, and regulatory challenges that currently limit their clinical implementation. Current evidence indicates that AI-based voice biomarkers have considerable potential for screening, diagnostic support, and longitudinal monitoring of neurological disorders, including Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease, multiple sclerosis, and other neurodegenerative conditions. Several studies report high diagnostic performance under controlled experimental settings. However, substantial heterogeneity in study design, sample size, languages, speech acquisition protocols, validation strategies, and reporting standards limits direct comparison between studies and hinders clinical translation. External validation and prospective multicenter studies remain scarce. AI-based voice analysis represents a promising, scalable, and non-invasive complement to conventional neurological assessment, with particular potential for remote screening and disease monitoring. Nevertheless, current evidence does not yet support routine clinical implementation. Future progress will depend on standardized speech acquisition protocols, robust external validation across diverse populations, explainable AI models, and regulatory frameworks capable of ensuring safety, reproducibility, and clinical reliability.

title: Immune checkpoints inhibitors in the treatment of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
journal: Neurological sciences : official journal of the Italian Neurological Society and of the Italian Society of Clinical Neurophysiology
abstract: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) is a rare but catastrophic demyelinating disease of the central nervous system (CNS) caused the JC virus (JCV). However, no effective treatments have been identified. Immune check point inhibitors (ICIs) are considered a potential treatment option. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to pool the data from the literature that evaluates the efficacy of using ICI in the treatment of PML. The search was conducted on January 24, 2026 using PubMed, Scopus, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), and Embase. Studies were included if they included patients with PML and evaluated the efficacy of using ICIs including PD-1, PD-L1, and CTLA-4 inhibitors in PML treatment. The exposure of interest was the use of ICI in the treatment of PML. The outcomes of interest were survival, disability and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) viral load. Rate and weighted mean difference (WMD) and their 95% confidence intervals (95%CI) were used as the effect size in the analysis. We included a total of 186 patients with PML from 52 articles. The survival rate among the included patients was 62% (95%CI: 52%-72%). There was no significant difference in disability between before and after the treatment with ICI (WMD =- 0.03; 95%CI: - 2.11-2.04). On the other hand, the treatment was associated with lower viral levels in the CSF (WMD = 69.20; 95%CI: 1.69-136.70). Future randomized clinical trials or comparative observational studies that investigate the efficacy of using ICI in the treatment of PML compared to other treatment modalities are needed.

title: Advances in plant polysaccharide research for neurodegenerative diseases therapy.
abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases (NDs), including Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), Huntington's disease (HD), amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), and multiple sclerosis (MS), represent a growing global public health burden with limited therapeutic options. Plant polysaccharides are natural, biocompatible, and multi-target bioactive macromolecules that have emerged as promising candidates for ND intervention. This review systematically summarizes recent progress in elucidating the structural characteristics, structure-activity relationships, and neuroprotective mechanisms of plant polysaccharides. Key structural features such as molecular weight, monosaccharide composition, glycosidic bond configuration, and spatial conformation critically modulate the biological activity of these molecules. Furthermore, we summarize the numerous protective effects of plant polysaccharides against NDs, including inhibiting abnormal protein aggregation, alleviating oxidative stress via the Nrf2/HO-1 pathway, suppressing neuroinflammation through the NF-κB and MAPK signaling pathways, regulating neuronal apoptosis, and modulating the gut-brain axis. Clinical translation challenges, primarily blood-brain barrier penetration, structural heterogeneity, and insufficient clinical validation, are discussed. Future directions include developing advanced delivery systems, conducting large-scale randomized controlled trials, and exploring synergistic combination therapies. Collectively, plant polysaccharides show considerable promise as potential multi-target candidates for the intervention of NDs, although further studies are needed to clarify their therapeutic potential and facilitate clinical translation.

title: CGRP levels in autoimmune diseases: a systematic review and meta-analysis of its potential role as a biomarker.
abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to quantitatively evaluate calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) concentrations across autoimmune diseases (psoriasis, rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, multiple sclerosis) and assess its clinical utility as a neuro-immune biofluid biomarker. PRISMA-compliant meta-analyses using random-effects models calculated standardized mean differences (SMDs, Hedges' g) from major databases, evaluating circulating biofluids (serum/plasma; 10 studies, 16 cohorts) both overall across all selected autoimmune diseases and stratified by individual disease entities, separately from localized compartments. Primary synthesis of circulating biofluids (533 cases, 363 controls) showed significant systemic CGRP elevation in autoimmune conditions (SMD = 0.63, 95% CI: 0.46-0.80, Circulating CGRP is elevated across specific autoimmune pathologies, functioning as a dynamic indicator of active neuro-immune inflammation rather than a static universal marker. Clinical implementation requires prospective, longitudinal studies and standardized, isoform-specific quantification assays. CRD420261458044.

title: Stereotactic radiosurgery for bilateral trigeminal neuralgia: A systematic review and proposed framework for staged treatment.
abstract: Bilateral trigeminal neuralgia (BTN) is uncommon and surgically complex. Stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) is a minimally invasive option for medically refractory BTN, although evidence remains sparse and heterogeneous. This systematic review evaluated the efficacy, durability, and toxicity of SRS in medically refractory BTN. It also synthesized the evidence into a practical staged-treatment framework. PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library were searched through October 11, 2026. Eligible studies reported BTN-specific SRS outcomes in adults, separately from unilateral cohorts. Two independent reviewers performed study selection, data extraction, and risk-of-bias assessment using adapted Newcastle-Ottawa and MINORS tools. Certainty of evidence was evaluated using a GRADE-informed approach. Owing to clinical heterogeneity and small samples, findings were synthesized narratively rather than by meta-analysis. Six reports met the inclusion criteria. Five described 88 BTN patients, including 54 SRS-treated patients across four reports. Of 91 nominally treated nerves, 67 were explicitly reported, and 24 were inferred from staged bilateral SRS in 12 patients. The sixth report described one BTN case without a complete subgroup denominator. Study-reported initial pain relief ranged from 71.4% to 100% across heterogeneous outcome definitions and analytical units. Pain recurrence was frequent, with durability varying markedly from 14 months to 1697 days in the sequential-onset series. Multiple sclerosis appeared associated with poorer outcomes and earlier recurrence, based on small subgroups. Repeat SRS achieved adequate pain relief in 10 of 11 retreated nerves (91%) in the largest cohort, with a median durability of 2.8 years. Sensory disturbance was the most common adverse event. One report described disabling bilateral numbness in a patient with prior bilateral ablative treatment. Anesthesia dolorosa incidence remains uncertain. SRS may provide early pain control in selected patients with medically refractory BTN, but bilateral sensory morbidity remains uncertain. Staged treatment was described in several reports, whereas bilateral treatment timing was unreported in one case. Certainty of evidence remains very low. Current evidence supports individualized decision-making focused on etiology, surgical fitness, first-side response, sensory toxicity, and cumulative bilateral trigeminal morbidity.Registration and Protocol: This systematic review was not registered in a prospective registry (e.g., PROSPERO). A protocol was developed a priori and is publicly available at https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/RBVNE.

title: Lower recorded prevalence of Alzheimer's disease in natalizumab-exposed older adults with multiple sclerosis: A hypothesis-generating observation.
abstract: Adaptive immune mechanisms, including CD8 T cell-mediated neuroinflammation, are increasingly implicated in Alzheimer's disease. We examined whether exposure to natalizumab, an α4-integrin antagonist that restricts leukocyte trafficking into the central nervous system, was associated with Alzheimer's disease prevalence among older adults with multiple sclerosis. Using Epic Cosmos electronic health record data, we identified 875,226 individuals with MS, of whom 9095 had an Alzheimer's disease diagnosis after age 65 years. Alzheimer's disease prevalence differed significantly across disease-modifying therapies, with natalizumab-treated patients demonstrating the lowest prevalence (0.13%; 95% confidence interval: 0.10-0.17%). These findings demonstrate a lower recorded prevalence of late-life Alzheimer's disease among natalizumab-exposed patients; however, given the aggregated nature of the data, this observation should be considered descriptive and hypothesis-generating.

title: Multiple sclerosis relapse redefined: Effect of an MRI-supported relapse criterion on ublituximab outcomes in the ULTIMATE I and II trials.
abstract: In relapsing multiple sclerosis trials, reductions in annualized relapse rate and gadolinium-enhancing lesions often diverge, potentially due to misclassification of pseudoexacerbations as relapses. We evaluated whether incorporating magnetic resonance imaging evidence into relapse definitions improves specificity and apparent treatment effect. We performed post hoc analyses of the ULTIMATE I and II phase 3 trials comparing ublituximab versus teriflunomide. Relapses were adjudicated per protocol (Expanded Disability Status Scale/Functional System Scales criteria). We applied increasingly stringent clinical criteria and a magnetic resonance imaging-supported relapse definition (new T2 lesion). Annualized relapse rate was modeled using a generalized estimating equation with exposure offset. Power/sample size implications were estimated. Protocol-defined annualized relapse rate reduction with ublituximab was 54.2% (annualized relapse rate: 0.084 vs 0.183). Stringent clinical criteria modestly increased reduction to 60.1%. Magnetic resonance imaging-supported relapses markedly amplified the effect to 87.5% (rate ratio: 0.125), with Year 2 reduction to 92.8%. Most ublituximab relapses (77.3%) lacked magnetic resonance imaging activity versus teriflunomide (17.8%). Power analyses indicated approximately a two-thirds sample size reduction using magnetic resonance imaging-supported relapses. Requiring magnetic resonance imaging evidence substantially increases specificity of relapse ascertainment, unmasks treatment effects of high-efficacy therapy, and improves trial efficiency. Prospective validation of magnetic resonance imaging-supported relapse definitions as complementary/alternative endpoints in relapsing multiple sclerosis trials is warranted, plus further corroboration with other biomarkers of disease activity toward a truly biologically verified relapse definition.

title: Attitudes towards vaccination in multiple sclerosis: insights from patients, neurologists, and general practitioners within a qualitative study.
abstract: People with Multiple Sclerosis (pwMS) face increased infection and mortality risks due to their disease and potentially immunosuppressive therapy. Comprehensive vaccination is recommended, but reported vaccination rates in pwMS vary, and concerns about safety und effectiveness are discussed as one possible reason. This study examines the vaccination rates and hesitancy in pwMS from the perspectives of patients, neurologists, and general practitioners (GPs) to identify possible approaches to overcome the hesitation. Between March and December 2023 narrative, semi-structured interviews were conducted with fifteen patients, five neurologists, and ten GPs in Germany. Pseudonymized data were analyzed using Kuckartz's Qualitative Content Analysis with MAXQDA, incorporating deductive and inductive codes. In total, thirty participants were interviewed. Our findings suggest that some pwMS experience gaps in vaccination-related information and desire more proactive information from physicians. Several participants described that communication between neurologists and GPs was limited and that it was not always clear which physician addresses vaccination counselling and administration. Fear of side effects and misinformation encountered by patients affect vaccination willingness. Patients prefer precise and consistent information materials on vaccination timelines. Misinformation or lack of information may contribute to vaccination reluctance. Addressing patients' concerns with comprehensible information appears to be an important element of vaccination counselling from the perspective of the participants. Our findings highlight the importance of improved communication and education among all parties involved in vaccination. German Register of Clinical Studies (DRKS): https://drks.de/search/de/trial/DRKS00031559 (Registration Date: 28.08.2023, retrospectively registered).

title: CD4(+) T cell subsets in CNS disorders: Pathogenic roles, immune dysregulation, and therapeutic perspectives.
abstract: The central nervous system (CNS), previously considered immune-isolated due to the blood-brain barrier (BBB) and absence of lymphatic drainage, is now understood as a dynamic interface with the peripheral immune system. CNS neurons and glia actively modulate immune responses, and circulating T cells survey and sometimes infiltrate this privileged site. While essential for host defense and tissue homeostasis, dysregulated immune surveillance may contribute to chronic neuroinflammation and, in specific disease contexts, autoimmune pathology. A key question is how T cell responses are initiated in the CNS, given its limited antigen presentation. This review synthesizes current evidence on the pathogenic and protective roles of Th1, Th2, Th17, and Treg cells across autoimmune demyelinating and neurodegenerative CNS disorders, with a focus on multiple sclerosis (MS), Alzheimer's disease (AD), and Parkinson's disease (PD). We also evaluate emerging T cell-targeted immunotherapies and their potential to rebalance CNS immunity and impede disease progression.

title: Hypothalamus-driven brain health through metabolic flexibility.
abstract: Organismal physiology depends on continuous, non-hierarchical communication among cells, tissues, and organs. We argue that this communication rests on metabolic flexibility-the capacity of cells and tissues to adapt substrate use to changing energetic demands-and that the hypothalamus serves as the central hub coordinating this flexibility across the body. Using hypothalamic agouti-related protein (AgRP) and pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) neurons as a model, we show these melanocortin neurons do more than regulate hunger and satiety: by integrating metabolic, hormonal, and immune signals, they shape reward, learning, executive function, and social behavior, while imposing coordinated metabolic states on peripheral tissues. When this flexibility is lost, as with aging or overnutrition, body-brain communication becomes rigid, driving cognitive decline, chronic inflammation, and neurodegenerative disease. We propose that signals from the body are not peripheral modifiers of brain function but fundamental determinants of it, with direct implications for hypothalamus-centered strategies to preserve brain health across the lifespan.

title: Uncovering disability progression in people with multiple sclerosis: a practical guide.
abstract: People with multiple sclerosis (pwMS) often experience disability progression even when receiving disease-modifying therapies that effectively suppress relapses. This phenomenon is commonly referred to as progression independent of relapse activity (PIRA). Currently, it is challenging to characterize pwMS who are experiencing disability progression in clinical practice. Existing definitions of PIRA rely primarily on the Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS), which is biased towards ambulation and does not effectively capture the gradual accumulation of symptoms and signs across other clinical areas associated with disability progression. Here, we propose a step-by-step approach that neurologists can use in clinical practice to identify pwMS experiencing disability progression irrespective of age, EDSS, or disease duration. By using this approach, neurologists can assess the presence or absence of specific variables to help determine if disability is stable or progressing. This could enable appropriate treatments to be implemented in a timely manner, particularly as new disability-targeting therapies become available.

title: Sexual Health in Females with Multiple Sclerosis of Reproductive Age.
abstract: Sexual dysfunction is highly prevalent among females with multiple sclerosis (FwMS), yet it remains under-recognized and inadequately integrated into routine care. This review examines sexual health in FwMS of reproductive age, with particular attention to assessment, reproductive considerations, and management. Sexual dysfunction in FwMS is often multifactorial, with contributions from neurological, physical, psychological, and relationship-related factors. Sexual dysfunction and disease-related factors may indirectly influence sexual activity, conception, and reproductive decision-making. Preconception counselling should incorporate sexual health alongside disease activity and treatment considerations. Evidence regarding sexual function during pregnancy and postpartum in FwMS remains limited. Management is individualized and may include symptom optimization, pelvic floor therapy, exercise, psychological and couples-based interventions, and selected pharmacologic therapies. Sexual health should be incorporated into comprehensive MS care, particularly during reproductive transitions. Prospective studies across preconception, pregnancy, and postpartum periods and randomized trials of interventions in FwMS are needed to guide evidence-based care.

title: Depression among patients with recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection: a nationwide inpatient analysis.
abstract: Using the National Inpatient Sample (2018-2019), we calculated depression rates among adults with recurrent CDI (rCDI) and assessed the odds of codiagnosed depression compared to other chronic medical conditions. Among 84,055 hospitalizations with rCDI, 21.5% had a codiagnosis of depression. In a population without CDI, depression prevalence was 14.2%. CDI patients had a 56% greater chance of having a diagnosis of depression compared with the general population (odds ratio [OR] 1.56, 95% confidence interval 1.5-1.6). When compared to those with common chronic medical comorbidities, patients with CDI had significantly higher odds of having depression than those with heart failure (OR 1.4), diabetes (OR 1.3), end-stage kidney disease (OR 1.5), and metastatic cancer (OR 1.9). Patients with fibromyalgia, multiple sclerosis, and alcohol-related disorders had higher rates of depression compared with those with CDI. Patients with rCDI appear to have remarkably high depression rates, higher than those of patients with many other common chronic medical conditions. Further studies are needed to evaluate the causation of this potential association and to consider the benefit of implementing depression screening programs in this vulnerable population.

title: Multiple Sclerosis, Depression, and Sex Differences: An Enduring Conundrum.
journal: The Journal of neuropsychiatry and clinical neurosciences
abstract: No clear sex difference in depressive symptoms has been observed among people with multiple sclerosis (MS), unlike for the general population in which females have higher depression rates. MS, however, is heterogeneous. The authors evaluated whether the influence of sex on depressive symptoms in MS varies across age, disease-related variables, or testing year. Data were gathered from 1,731 adults with MS assessed at a neuropsychiatry clinic between 2006 and 2025 and stratified by age (18-45, 46-55, and ≥56 years), disease duration (0-4, 5-9, and ≥10 years), Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) scores (0.0-1.0, 1.5-2.5, and ≥3.0), illness subtype (primary progressive, secondary progressive, and relapsing remitting), and testing year (2006-2015, 2016-2020, and 2021-2025). Depressive symptoms were measured with the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale depression subscale (HADS-D). Analyses of covariance, controlled for education, were conducted to test for a sex difference in HADS-D scores and whether the influence of sex varied according to stratified subgroups. The mean±SD participant age was 43.5±11.0 years; 73% were women; and the median EDSS score was 2.0 (interquartile range 1.5-3.5). HADS-D scores did not significantly differ between men (mean=7.2±4.2) and women (mean=6.9±4.0). In analyses controlled for education, the effect of sex on HADS-D scores did not significantly differ by age (η Across various disease-related characteristics and cross-sectional periods, depressive symptoms did not significantly differ between men and women with MS.

title: Effect of Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (rTMS) on Serum Neurofilament Light Chain (sNfL) and its Correlation to Cognitive Function in Multiple Sclerosis.
abstract: BackgroundTranscranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) is a non-invasive neuromodulatory technique that has emerged as a promising therapeutic intervention for various neurological disorders by modulating cortical excitability and neural plasticity. Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic inflammatory demyelinating condition marked by central nervous system (CNS) lesions that can cause significant physical or cognitive disability, as well as neurological abnormalities. We now know that 40-70% of all MS patients have cognitive impairment that impairs their lives. Even in these so-called benign forms of the disease, 15 years after diagnosis, with an Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) score of up to 3, cognitive abnormalities can be diagnosed in half of these patients.ObjectiveTo investigate whether high frequency (rTMS) can modify MS cognition assessed by clinical and serum Neurofilament Light Chain (sNfL).MethodsForty-five patients with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS) were randomly allocated into three equal groups (n = 15 each): a 5-Hz rTMS group, an 18-Hz rTMS group, and a sham stimulation group. The treatment protocols were administered daily on five consecutive days weekly for 2 weeks over the vertex and left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (lt. DLPFC). Cognitive performance was assessed using the Brief International Cognitive Assessment for Multiple Sclerosis (BICAMS), comprising the Symbol Digit Modalities Test (SDMT), California Verbal Learning Test-Second Edition (CVLT-II), and Brief Visuospatial Memory Test-Revised (BVMT-R). Serum neurofilament light chain (sNfL) levels were measured as the secondary outcome.ResultsRepeated-measures ANOVA demonstrated significant time, group, and time-by-group interaction effects for sustained attention (SDMT), verbal learning and memory (CVLT-II), and visuospatial memory and learning (BVMT-R) (all

title: Adherence System Usability Patient Experience and Psychosocial Impact in Robot Assisted Gait Neurorehabilitation A Cross Sectional Study.
abstract: BackgroundAttendance, usability and rehabilitation experience may relate to perceived psychosocial impact in robotic neurorehabilitation.ObjectiveTo examine these associations in adults receiving robot-assisted gait neurorehabilitation, including diagnosis-adjusted and exploratory indirect associations.MethodsThis single-center observational study included 250 adults with stroke, spinal cord injury, multiple sclerosis or cerebral palsy. The System Usability Scale (SUS), Neurorehabilitation Experience Questionnaire (NREQ) and Psychosocial Impact of Assistive Devices Scale (PIADS) were administered in week two. Attendance covered the planned course; participation equaled attended/planned sessions × 100. Analyses included Spearman correlations, adjusted regression, indirect-association models with 5,000 bootstrap resamples, Kruskal-Wallis tests and Cronbach's alpha.ResultsMean participation was 86.35 ± 8.38%. Mean SUS, NREQ and PIADS scores were 72.79 ± 12.06, 27.84 ± 4.92 and 1.67 ± 0.74, respectively. Adherence correlated with SUS (r

title: Development of a smartphone-derived digital gait impairment score referenced to healthy controls in multiple sclerosis.
abstract: Smartphone gait assessments generate numerous features that are difficult to summarize as clinically interpretable measures in multiple sclerosis (MS). To develop and internally evaluate a healthy-control-referenced digital gait impairment score. In this cross-sectional study, 66 participants with MS and 101 healthy controls (HC) completed a standardized smartphone task comprising 20-step outbound and return walks. From 4128 sensor-derived features, 50 were selected based on their associations with Timed 25-Foot Walk (T25FW) in MS, normalized using age- and sex-adjusted HC models, and averaged to construct a single digital gait impairment score. Group differences and correlations with T25FW, Multiple Sclerosis Walking Scale-12 (MSWS-12), and Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) were evaluated. Internal validation used repeated five-fold cross-validation, reconstructing the score within training folds. Additional analyses examined whether the score added information about MSWS-12 and EDSS beyond T25FW, accounting for age and sex. In the full-cohort analysis, the score was higher in MS than in HC (adjusted β = 0.41; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.20-0.61). Spearman correlations with T25FW, MSWS-12, and EDSS were 0.58 (95% CI 0.38, 0.73), 0.45 (95% CI 0.23, 0.63), and 0.43 (95% CI 0.20, 0.60), respectively. Across 29/50 evaluable cross-validation repeats, corresponding median correlations were 0.49, 0.40, and 0.36. The score added little information about MSWS-12 or EDSS beyond age, sex, and T25FW. This study provides proof of concept for quantifying deviations from expected healthy gait in MS. The score remains developmental and requires refinement, external validation, and longitudinal evaluation before routine clinical use.

title: Catastrophic out-of-pocket (OOP) expenditure and perceived financial burden among people with multiple sclerosis in Egypt: A multicenter cross-sectional study.
abstract: People with multiple sclerosis (PwMS) in Egypt receive governmental coverage for disease-modifying therapies (DMTs), yet they continue to face considerable out-of-pocket (OOP) expenses for supportive care and monitoring. Data on catastrophic OOP expenditure in the region are lacking. This study assessed the prevalence and predictors of catastrophic OOP expenditure and the associated perceived financial burden among PwMS in Egypt. A multicenter cross-sectional study was conducted among adult PwMS attending MS clinics at three tertiary university hospitals (Alexandria, Ain Shams, and Tanta) in Egypt. Participants completed a structured questionnaire assessing sociodemographic characteristics, clinical features, disease-related factors, and MS-related OOP healthcare expenditure during the preceding year. Catastrophic expenditure was assessed using three thresholds of OOP spending relative to household income: ≥10%, ≥25%, and ≥40%. Because household income was collected categorically, lower-bound, midpoint, and upper-bound income estimates were evaluated, with the midpoint estimate used for the primary analysis. Multivariable modified Poisson regression models with robust variance estimation were performed to identify independent predictors of COPE, and results were reported as adjusted prevalence ratios (aPRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Among 634 included PwMS, the median monthly OOP expenditure was 1,895.83 Egyptian pounds (IQR 929.17-3,587.50), corresponding to a median OOP-to-household-income ratio of 0.43 using the midpoint income estimate. Under the primary analysis, 589 participants (92.9%) experienced OOP expenditure ≥10% of household income, 478 (75.4%) exceeded the ≥25% threshold, and 343 (54.1%) exceeded the ≥40% threshold. Perceived financial burden was highly prevalent and differed significantly across income groups at all expenditure thresholds (P<0.001). In multivariable analyses, recent relapse activity was consistently associated with a higher prevalence of COPE across all thresholds (≥10%: aPR 1.23, 95% CI 1.15-1.32; ≥25%: aPR 1.53, 95% CI 1.35-1.74; ≥40%: aPR 1.64, 95% CI 1.37-1.97). Older age was associated with higher prevalence of ≥25% and ≥40% COPE, while female sex was independently associated with ≥40% COPE (aPR 1.31, 95% CI 1.10-1.55). Catastrophic OOP healthcare expenditure is highly prevalent among PwMS in Egypt, affecting patients across socioeconomic categories and persisting across different expenditure thresholds. Disease activity and demographic factors contribute to increased financial vulnerability. Expanding financial protection beyond disease-modifying therapies to include investigations, rehabilitation, symptomatic treatments, and supportive services is essential to reduce the financial burden of MS and improve equitable access to comprehensive care.

title: A four-gene diagnostic panel for distinguishing primary progressive multiple sclerosis from HTLV-1-associated myelopathy/tropical spastic paraparesis.
abstract: Primary Progressive Multiple Sclerosis (PPMS) and HTLV-1-Associated Myelopathy/Tropical Spastic Paraparesis (HAM/TSP) are clinically overlapping progressive myelopathies characterized by spastic paraparesis and autonomic dysfunction. However, they originate from fundamentally distinct pathogenic processes: autoimmune demyelination in PPMS versus chronic retroviral-driven neuroinflammation in HAM/TSP. Current diagnostic approaches are frequently inadequate, as HTLV-1 screening is often omitted in non-endemic regions and positive serology in endemic areas does not rule out concomitant PPMS, highlighting the urgent need for complementary molecular diagnostic tools. In this study, we developed an integrative bioinformatics framework combining network analysis, differential expression profiling, and machine learning to identify a transcriptional signature capable of distinguishing PPMS from HAM/TSP. Disease-specific gene modules were identified through cross-dataset preservation analysis and module-trait correlations. Random Forest classification with recursive feature elimination was employed to derive a parsimonious Diagnostic Risk Score (DRS), which was validated on an independent external cohort under a frozen-threshold, leakage-free design. Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis (WGCNA) revealed striking topological divergence between the two diseases: HAM/TSP exhibited a consolidated network architecture with a single dominant module, whereas PPMS displayed a highly fragmented topology with numerous smaller modules. Cross-dataset preservation analysis identified 11 PPMS-specific and 63 HAM/TSP-specific candidate biomarker genes. Machine learning refinement reduced this to a 4-gene signature comprising ZFAND1, MAPRE2, TBK1, and LPAR6, which achieved robust classification performance in cross-validation (macro-averaged accuracy: 0.982; macro-averaged F1-score: 0.987; AUC-ROC: 0.995) and robust performance on external validation (macro-averaged accuracy: 0.975; macro-averaged F1-score: 0.937; AUC-ROC: 0.800). The 4-gene signature captures distinct biological dimensions: ZFAND1 marks proteostatic stress from viral inflammation, TBK1 excludes the HTLV-1 interferon signature, MAPRE2 reflects a HAM/TSP-associated cytoskeletal program, and LPAR6 links inflammatory signaling to oligodendrocyte maturation. This multidimensional architecture explains the panel's high accuracy and offers mechanistic insights. The proposed approach offers a practical, transcriptome-based adjunct to current diagnostic methods, with potential to guide therapeutic stratification and reduce misdiagnosis of PPMS and HAM/TSP.

title: Critical advances and translational bottlenecks of gut microbiota-gut-brain axis targeted therapy for neurodegenerative and neurodevelopmental disorders.
abstract: Neurological diseases have become a major global public health burden. Existing central nervous system-targeted therapies can only alleviate clinical symptoms but fail to halt the progression of neurodegenerative diseases, presenting mechanistic limitations and therapeutic bottlenecks. The gut microbiota participates in the regulation of central nervous system (CNS) homeostasis and neuropathological processes via the microbiota-gut-brain axis (MGBA). Notably, dysbiosis may induce damage to the blood-brain barrier, neurotransmitter dysregulation, and immune imbalance, thereby mediating the onset and progression of various neurological diseases, including Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease (AD), autism spectrum disorder (ASD), and multiple sclerosis (MS). This article provides a systematic review of the core mechanisms by which the gut microbiome regulates neurological diseases, including inflammation regulation, oxidative stress responses, and neuroendocrine remodeling mediated by microbial metabolites. It also comprehensively summarizes the research progress, application advantages, and existing limitations of novel gut-targeted interventions, such as probiotics, prebiotics, fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT), dietary interventions, and live biological therapies. At the same time, the article critically examines key bottlenecks prevalent in the field: the causal relationship between the microbiota and disease remains unclear; there is a significant translational gap between animal and human studies; there is a lack of unified standards for multi-omics analysis systems; and interference from confounding factors such as age, diet, and medications is significant. Existing research indicates that gut microbiota interventions complement traditional symptomatic treatments and hold promising prospects for early disease intervention and adjunctive therapy for refractory patients. Future efforts should integrate multi-omics and artificial intelligence technologies to decipher the causal networks governing gut-central nervous system regulation, establish standardized research frameworks, advance the clinical translation of precision gut microbiota therapies, and provide new approaches for the comprehensive prevention, control, and personalized treatment of neurological disorders.

title: Phytomicronutrients in neurodegeneration: modulating microglial dynamics for neuroprotection.
journal: Zeitschrift fur Naturforschung. C, Journal of biosciences
abstract: Microglial dysfunction plays a critical role in the pathophysiology of several neurodegenerative diseases, including multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's disease, and Alzheimer's disease. Emerging evidence suggests that targeting microglial activation could be a promising therapeutic strategy. This review critically examines recent studies investigating the effects of medicinal plant extracts and their bioactive compounds on microglial function. Relevant data from experimental and preclinical studies were analyzed to assess their neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory potential. Phytochemicals that are found in plants, especially flavonoids, alkaloids, and terpenoids, demonstrate important modulatory effects on microglials. These compounds control microglial polarization, inhibit the release of proinflammatory cytokines, and alleviate oxidative stress, thus, alleviating neuroinflammation and enhancing neuro-restoration. The results suggest that medicine plant extracts have effects on major molecular pathways associated with neuroinflammation, which provide new adjunctive treatment to neurodegenerative diseases. Nevertheless, there are still problems in the translation of these preclinical successes into clinical practice. The limited bioavailability, variability in phytochemical composition, and the absence of standardized formulations are some of the challenges that discourage clinical use. Also, thorough safety assessments should be conducted to achieve therapeutic effectiveness with no adverse effects. The medicinal plants and their bioactive compounds hold potential promise in regulating the dysfunction of microglia and in decreasing neuroinflammation. Future studies are needed to enhance the pharmacokinetic characteristics, to provide consistency in formulations, and to perform stringent clinical studies that would substantiate these findings and allow their use in therapeutic regimens of neuroinflammatory disorders.

title: Establishing Potosi Virus as a Human Pathogen: Fatal Neuroinvasive Disease in a B-Cell-Depleted Patient.
abstract: To establish Potosi virus, a mosquito-borne member of the family Case report. A 37-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis on long-term rituximab developed rapidly progressive dementia. Serial MRI demonstrated progressive generalized atrophy. CSF showed transient, minimal lymphocytic pleocytosis. Extensive infectious, autoimmune, and prion evaluations were unrevealing, but CSF metagenomic sequencing detected all 3 genome segments for Potosi virus. Postmortem examination revealed diffuse meningoencephalitis with T-cell-predominant leptomeningeal and perivascular inflammation. Molecular analyses confirmed multiple nucleotide sequences with >99+% concordance with a known Potosi strain, with widespread viral infection confirmed by immunohistochemistry demonstrating intracellular and extracellular viral antigen. Electron microscopy demonstrated particles of a size consistent with the Potosi virus can cause fatal neuroinvasive disease in humans, as evidenced by convergent postmortem neuropathologic, molecular, and ultrastructural evidence. Chronic B-cell depletion may increase susceptibility to severe disease with arboviral infections, which may present without conventional CNS inflammatory markers. CSF metagenomic sequencing should be considered in immunocompromised patients with unexplained progressive neurologic decline.

title: Affordability and relative economic burden of multiple sclerosis biologics in South America: a cross-country analysis of prices, purchasing power and regulatory access.
journal: Expert review of pharmacoeconomics & outcomes research
abstract: High-cost biological therapies for multiple sclerosis (MS) may have lower nominal prices in middle-income countries yet impose greater burden relative to local purchasing capacity. We compared regulatory availability, price transparency and relative economic burden. We analyzed alemtuzumab, interferon beta-1a, natalizumab and ocrelizumab in Brazil, Colombia, Peru and the United States. Prices were compared in nominal US dollars, purchasing power parity-adjusted international dollars and against minimum wages. Defined daily doses supported standardized comparisons; regimen-based costs used reference dosing schedules. Outcomes included historical marketing authorization, observable prices, wage-based affordability and annual acquisition cost relative to gross domestic product per capita. Historical marketing authorization was documented in all 16 medicine-country combinations (100%), and observable prices were identified in 14 (87.5%). None of the 14 assessable combinations met the adapted regimen-based affordability criterion. Under primary price scenarios, monthly-equivalent burden ranged from 27.2 calendar-day equivalents of statutory minimum-wage income for interferon beta-1a in Peru to 326.2 for alemtuzumab in Brazil. Although US nominal prices were generally highest, purchasing-power and wage adjustment altered country rankings. Historical marketing authorization and lower nominal prices did not imply economic accessibility. Cross-country assessments should integrate purchasing power, wages and regimen-based acquisition costs.

title: Emergence of natalizumab anti-drug antibodies during extended interval dosing in a patient with multiple sclerosis: A case report.
abstract: We present a natalizumab-treated patient with multiple sclerosis (MS) who developed neutralizing anti-drug antibodies (ADAs) after years of treatment following introduction of extended interval dosing (EID). To gain insight into how this sudden ADA development occurred. A pharmacokinetic model was used to evaluate the relation between natalizumab concentration and ADA production. EID from 4 to 6 weeks resulted in unexpectedly low natalizumab trough concentrations accompanied by increasing ADAs. Modeling suggested ADA production was stimulated by declining natalizumab concentrations. EID may result in increased ADA production, causing ADA-mediated clearance of natalizumab and risking new MS activity.

title: The role of microglia in remyelination: Mechanisms and therapeutic implications in multiple sclerosis.
abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic demyelinating disease of the central nervous system, accompanied by progressive neurological deficits. Current MS disease-modifying drugs mainly target peripheral immune cells and have demonstrated little efficacy for neuroprotection or remyelination. Growing evidence indicates that microglia play a critical dual role in demyelinating animal models and MS. In acute inflammatory phases, microglia adopt a pro-inflammatory phenotype, exacerbating demyelination and neural damage. But, as lesions evolve, these resident immune cells can transform into an anti-inflammatory state, promoting tissue repair and myelin regeneration. Despite the importance of microglia, the regulatory mechanism of this double-edged sword during demyelination and remyelination has not been fully elucidated. This review first provides an overview of the involvement of microglia in demyelination and remyelination, and how their functional evolution depends on disease stage, on the spatial location of the lesion and its microenvironment. Secondly, the interaction between microglia and astrocytes, monocyte-derived macrophages, T cells, and B cells is described, working together to balance the disrupted microenvironment, promote the formation, differentiation, and maturation of oligodendrocyte precursor cells, and ultimately achieve myelin protection and regeneration. We then organize the signaling pathways targeting microglia and remyelination, providing a theoretical basis for drug development. Finally, we present drugs or small-molecule compounds targeting signaling pathways for exploratory therapeutic research at different stages. In summary, this review highlights the importance of remyelination, microglial heterogeneity, the temporal nature of regulation, and the complexity of treatment. We also present some challenges and solutions for remyelination, providing valuable information for neurological recovery in MS patients.

title: Culturally adapted exercise training intervention for Hispanics/Latinos with multiple sclerosis: Study protocol for a hybrid type 1 implementation randomized controlled trial.
abstract: Hispanics with multiple sclerosis (MS) have worse walking mobility and health-related quality of life (QOL) than non-Hispanic white counterparts. Hispanics further receive less specialty care and have low physical activity rates. Exercise training can improve MS symptoms, including mobility and QOL, but there are few RCTs of exercise training programs in Hispanics with MS. The moVement for Advancing Mobility and Strength in MS (VAMOS-MS) study is a hybrid type 1 implementation randomized control trial that culturally adapts the Guidelines for Exercise in MS (GEMS) intervention for Hispanics with MS. The primary outcome is walking dysfunction, measured using the MSWS-12; the secondary outcome is Health-Related QOL (HRQOL), measured by the MSIS-29. Implementation outcomes include measures of Acceptability, Appropriateness, Feasibility, Adoption, and Sustainability. Exercise behavior will be measured using the Godin Leisure Time Exercise Questionnaire (GLTEQ). Following the baseline assessment, participants will be randomized to the 16-week GEMS exercise training condition or the 16-week waitlist control. Participants will receive materials, equipment, and coaching calls with a trained Community Health worker (CHW). Outcomes will be measured at baseline, 16 weeks, and 32 weeks. The data analysis will be conducted using the intent-to-treat principle, with linear mixed models including an interaction term between condition and time. Implementation outcomes will be analyzed using descriptive and qualitative methods. VAMOS-MS is a culturally adapted, home-based exercise training program for Hispanics with MS. It incorporates community feedback to inform the adaptation and implementation of an evidence-based exercise training program for scalability among Hispanics with MS.

title: Remibrutinib (Rhapsido(®)), a covalent Bruton's tyrosine kinase inhibitor approved for chronic spontaneous urticaria.
