title: Astragalus Polysaccharide Exerts a Neuroprotective Effect in a Demyelination Model by Alleviating Oxidative Stress.
abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an autoimmune disease of the central nervous system characterized by progressive demyelination and neurodegenerative damage. The accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and the resulting oxidative stress are considered key contributors to myelin injury and disease progression. Astragalus polysaccharide (APS), a water-soluble polysaccharide, exhibits multiple pharmacological activities, including immunomodulatory, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and anti-apoptotic effects. This study aimed to investigate the therapeutic effects of APS in MS and to explore its potential mechanisms. In vivo, APS was administered intraperitoneally at 50 mg/kg/day in a cuprizone-induced demyelinating mouse model, and its effects were evaluated by immunofluorescence, immunohistochemistry, and Western blotting. In vitro, the regulatory effects of APS on oxidative stress in oligodendrocytes were assessed by immunofluorescence and Western blotting in an H

title: The Emerging Role of Optogenetics in Multiple Sclerosis Research.
abstract: Optogenetics is a technique that uses light to manipulate genetically targeted neurons and has a potential role in the treatment of multiple sclerosis (MS). This review aims to examine how findings from current cell and animal studies in optogenetics may inform and advance future research in MS in humans. We conducted a narrative literature review of in vivo and in vitro animal studies investigating optogenetic applications in MS, focusing on their potential to enhance therapeutic outcomes. Our review generated 58 articles related to our topic, and 9 of them were included. Optogenetics enhances remyelination by promoting the differentiation of oligodendrocyte precursor cells into myelinating cells, thereby easing neural repair in demyelinated regions and restoring normal cognitive function in the animal model of MS. In addition, optogenetics offers valuable insights into MS by enabling the study of specific gene mutations, such as heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein A1, paving the way for novel therapeutic strategies. This review discusses the future of optogenetics as a potential treatment for MS. This innovative technology may offer an improved approach to managing the disease, offering refined control over drug delivery, remyelination, and gene therapy. Further research should prioritize optimizing these technologies for clinical use and exploring their potential in combination therapies to improve patient outcomes. More research is also needed to reassess any complications or restrictions associated with optogenetics.

title: Lived Experiences of Bladder and Bowel Dysfunction for People With Multiple Sclerosis and Their Providers: A Qualitative Meta-Synthesis.
abstract: Bladder dysfunction and bowel dysfunction impact up to 80% of individuals with multiple sclerosis (MS). Beyond their physical effects, they can reduce quality of life and contribute to emotional distress for people with MS. Exploring the nuanced, lived experiences of people with MS who have bladder and/or bowel dysfunction is critical to better understanding these challenges. The purpose of this meta-synthesis was to answer the following research question: What are the lived experiences of bladder and bowel dysfunction for people with MS and their clinicians? This qualitative meta-synthesis included a comprehensive literature search of 3 databases. Titles, abstracts, and full texts were reviewed by 2 reviewers. Included articles were critically appraised, and reciprocal translation was used to synthesize novel, representative themes from the primary studies. Systematic searches yielded 3664 articles, of which 14 met the inclusion criteria. Three themes were identified: quality-of-life impacts, barriers to accessing health care (subthemes: clinician-driven access barriers, patient-driven access barriers, opportunities for facilitating access to bladder and/or bowel health care), and symptom management strategies. Findings highlight patient embarrassment surrounding bladder and bowel symptoms, limited clinician engagement, and low awareness of intervention options from both people with MS and their clinicians. More research is needed to improve educational interventions, increase access to specialized health care, and understand the perspectives of people with MS and bladder and bowel dysfunction in differing health care systems.

title: Examining the Relationship Between Perceived Social Satisfaction, Depression, and Anxiety for People With Multiple Sclerosis Participating in Group Treatment Modalities.
abstract: This study examined group therapy as a treatment modality for people with multiple sclerosis (MS). Specifically, social satisfaction, anxiety, and depression outcomes were explored in relation to treatment modalities. A retrospective cohort study was conducted to examine the relationship between social satisfaction, anxiety, and depression for people with MS in group vs individual therapy. Inclusion criteria were age of 18 years or older, MS diagnosis, and participation in 3 or more group (intervention) or individual (control) therapy sessions with an MS behavioral medicine clinician. Participants completed the Quality of Life in Neurological Disorders (Neuro-QOL), Patient Health Questionnaire 9-item, and Generalized Anxiety Disorder 7-item scales. Demographic variables and disease characteristics were also examined in the context of treatment modalities and in relation to reported social satisfaction. Multivariable linear regression models were constructed. In covariate-adjusted models, baseline Neuro-QOL social satisfaction Anxiety and depression are negatively associated with social satisfaction, and treatment type is not associated with differing social satisfaction scores. Given this, patient-reported social satisfaction is an important consideration in the clinical treatment and interdisciplinary management of MS. Additional research is warranted to better understand outcomes relevant to different treatment modalities.

title: Radial Extracorporeal Shock Wave Therapy for Triceps Surae Spasticity in People With Multiple Sclerosis: A Pilot Study.
abstract: Spasticity represents a major symptom of people with multiple sclerosis (MS), frequently causing disability, pain, and abnormal postures. The aim of this study is the evaluation of safety and efficacy of radial extracorporeal shock wave therapy (RESWT) for triceps surae muscle spastic hypertonia in people with MS. Two centers recruited people 18 years or older with MS and triceps surae muscle hypertonia. People were excluded if they had other neurological conditions; had used anticoagulants; had intrathecal baclofen, botulinum toxin, and/or physiotherapy within the past 8 months; or had oral antispasmodics therapy modification in the past 4 weeks. The participants underwent triceps surae RESWT once a week for 4 weeks. Participants were scored on the Modified Ashworth Scale (MAS), the Numerical Rating Scale for spasticity (NRS-Sp), the Medical Research Council (MRC) scale, the Timed Up and Go (TUG) test, and the Timed 25-Foot Walk (T25-FW) test before RESWT (T0) and immediately after RESWT (T1). Self-perceived effect was evaluated via the Global Perceived Effect (GPE) at T1. Twenty-six people with MS were included (10 women and 16 men; mean age ± SD, 52.46 ± 8.39 years; mean Expanded Disability Status Scale score ± SD, 5.44 ± 1.34; mean disease duration ± SD, 14.88 ± 10.83 years), and 36 triceps surae were treated. MAS and NRS-Sp scores decreased at T1, whereas TUG, T25-FW, and MRC scores were comparable over time. Via the GPE, 73% of participants reported a self-perceived positive effect of RESWT on spasticity. RESWT may be efficacious and safe for treating spasticity in people with MS and does not adversely affect gait, strength, or dynamic balance. Further long-term studies are needed to evaluate the possibility of using RESWT as a treatment for spasticity in people with MS.

title: Exploring Factors and Nonpharmacological Interventions Associated With Respiratory Function in People With Multiple Sclerosis: A Scoping Review.
abstract: Abstract. Multiple sclerosis (MS) can impair respiratory function due to demyelinating lesions that disrupt neural input to respiratory muscles. This dysfunction may result in muscular weakness, ineffective coughing, and respiratory failure. Early identification and management of respiratory dysfunction can improve long-term outcomes and reduce morbidity and mortality. Factors contributing to early respiratory decline in MS are understudied. This review aims to characterize factors associated with and nonpharmacological interventions for respiratory dysfunction in people with MS. This review was registered with the Open Science Framework and conducted in accordance with Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews guidelines. A comprehensive search of PubMed, Embase, and Scopus was conducted for articles published in English between 2014 and 2024. Eligible studies assessed respiratory function and evaluated nonpharmacological interventions or associated factors. Peer-reviewed observational and experimental studies were included. Titles, abstracts, and full texts were screened independently by 2 reviewers using Covidence. Findings from 11 observational studies identified factors that influence respiratory function, including disease-related, physical, and psychological factors. Nine studies investigated nonpharmacological interventions such as inspiratory/expiratory muscle training, Pilates, lung volume recruitment, and proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation; all showed improvements in respiratory outcomes. Although the impact of physiological, functional, psychological, and psychosocial factors has been studied in relation to respiratory dysfunction in MS, other increasingly common factors in MS, such as obesity, have not been studied and warrant further investigation. Nonpharmacological therapies show promise in improving respiratory function in people with MS, but larger trials with longer-duration interventions are needed to confirm the efficacy of these interventions.

title: A Positive Psychology Intervention for People With New Diagnoses of Multiple Sclerosis: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
abstract: The period surrounding the diagnosis of multiple sclerosis (MS) is physically and emotionally challenging. Positive psychology (PP) exercises (ie, systematic activities to cultivate well-being) have been shown to increase positive emotional responses, such as positive affect, and may aid in psychosocial adjustment to MS. Participants were randomly asigned 1:1 to a 5-week, at-home, self-directed PP intervention or a waitlist control condition. The PP intervention consisted of 5 previously tested PP exercises. Feasibility was defined as the proportion of participants who completed at least 4 of the 5 PP exercises. Acceptability was determined by participant ratings of ease and utility (0-10 scale) reported at the completion of each exercise. The effects of the PP intervention on a battery of patient-reported outcome measures were also examined using linear mixed-effects models. Thirty participants were enrolled in the study, and 70% met the a priori threshold for feasibility. Mean ease scores across the exercises ranged from 7.0 to 7.9 (scale of 0-10), and mean utility scores ranged from 7.0 to 8.1. There were statistically significant increases in positive affect (6.68; 95% CI, 2.58-10.78; A 5-week at-home self-directed PP intervention was feasible and acceptable to individuals with new diagnoses of MS. Larger trials with longer follow-up are needed to fully understand the benefits of PP training to improve adjustment to MS diagnosis, which may lead to better psychosocial and health outcomes.

title: Mesenchymal stromal cells for progressive multiple sclerosis: current evidence and translational challenges.
abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an autoimmune disease of the central nervous system (CNS) characterized by demyelinating lesions leading to cumulative and irreversible neurological damage. In the progressive form of MS (PMS), pathogenic mechanisms are multifaceted, involving both compartmentalized inflammation and neurodegeneration. Owing to their immunomodulatory and trophic properties, mesenchymal stromal cells (MSC) have emerged as a promising therapeutic strategy for this patient population. To review the relevant immunomodulatory and neuroprotective mechanisms of MSC demonstrated in vitro, summarize preclinical and clinical evidence regarding MSC safety and efficacy in experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) murine model and in MS, and discuss key challenges hindering clinical translation. MSC display combined immunomodulatory and neuroprotective properties that are particularly relevant in MS. They induce sustained immune reprogramming of T cells, B cells, and myeloid cells, through paracrine signaling, extracellular vesicle release, metabolic modulation, and efferocytosis of apoptotic cells. These effects are influenced by the local microenvironment, MSC tissue source, manufacturing processes, and route of administration. Beyond immune regulation, MSC promote CNS repair by secreting neurotrophic and angiogenic factors and through mitochondrial transfer. In chronic EAE models, MSC consistently reduce disease severity, mitigate CNS inflammation, and promote neuroprotection, with enhanced efficacy following intrathecal or intraventricular administration. Early-phase clinical trials in PMS have demonstrated a favorable safety profile but inconsistent efficacy, likely reflecting substantial heterogeneity in study design, cell products, dosing regimens, and administration routes. Nevertheless, emerging evidence suggests that repeated intrathecal administration and improved patient stratification may optimize therapeutic outcomes. MSC-based therapies represent a potentially valuable avenue for PMS. However, their clinical benefit remains to be firmly established, pending well-designed trials addressing product standardization, optimized delivery approaches, and the use of robust, clinically meaningful endpoints.

title: Deciphering the mechanistic landscape of notch signaling in autoimmune pathogenesis.
abstract: Autoimmune diseases are a group of disorders with multiple etiologies that disrupt normal immunological function, leading to the immune system mistakenly attacking the body's own tissues. The Notch signaling pathway is a conserved pathway that is in part responsible for multiple cellular behaviors, including proliferation, differentiation, development, and death, through direct cell-to-cell communication. The expression and activation of Notch signaling pathway proteins are aberrantly regulated in autoimmune diseases in a manner that is closely related to their onset and development. We reviewed the functioning of the Notch signaling pathway in several autoimmune disorders, including rheumatoid arthritis (RA), systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), primary Sjögren's syndrome (pSS), juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA), idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), multiple sclerosis (MS), autoimmune vasculitis, autoimmune hepatitis (AIH), autoimmune thyroid disease (AITD), autoimmune kidney diseases and type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM). We specifically sought to explore the involvement of the Notch signaling pathway in the occurrence and progression of RA to provide ideas and approaches for developing new therapeutic strategies for this autoimmune disease.

title: Pilot Study of Smartphone-Based Neuroperformance Tests in Multiple Sclerosis.
abstract: The Multiple Sclerosis Functional Composite and its iPad-based companion, the Multiple Sclerosis Performance Test (MSPT), as well as other traditional function tests must be performed during a clinic visit, which presents challenges for some people with multiple sclerosis (MS). Smartphone tests were developed, including a remote Timed Up and Go (rTUG), remote 5 Times Sit-to-Stand (r5STS), finger tapping test (FTT), and processing speed test (PST), in addition to open- and closed-eye balance measures. People with MS and a control group (CG) without MS performed smartphone tests and the previously validated, iPad-based MSPT. Convergent validity, sensitivity to disease status, and test-retest reliability were assessed. The CG (n = 23; mean age, 38.56 ± 18.5 years; 65% female; 74% White) and the MS group (n = 23; mean age, 58.5 ± 11.9 years; 48% female; 83% White; mean disease duration, 11.82 ± 6.72 years) completed tests at a single visit. Valid taps per second on FTT was moderately correlated with the manual dexterity test (Spearman correlation coefficients, ρ = -0.46 [right] and -0.41 [left]). Total number correct on smartphone-administered PST strongly correlated with iPad-administered PST (ρ = 0.78). rTUG had a strong correlation and r5STS had a moderate correlation with the Timed 25-Foot Walk test (ρ = 0.80 and 0.55, respectively). Ellipse volume and ellipse area, derived from open-eye balance tests, showed sensitivity to disease status (partial η2 = 0.08 and 0.07, respectively) and good test-retest reliability (intraclass correlation coefficient = 0.82 and 0.77, respectively). The FTT, PST, rTUG, and r5STS performed via smartphone application demonstrate convergent validity with their analogous MSPT tests. Open-eye balance outcomes also show promise for use in people with MS. These smartphone-based tests may allow for remote measurement of function for people with MS.

title: Outcomes of Comprehensive Multiple Sclerosis Care: A Pilot Comparison of Intensive, Integrated, and Usual Care Approaches.
abstract: A comprehensive personalized care approach may better support individuals with multiple sclerosis (MS) in managing their health, function, and quality of life than clinical care that does not incorporate evidence-based, comprehensive, and personalized care. This pilot study compared outcomes among people with MS who participated in a 4-day comprehensive MS care program, those treated in an MS institute, and those who received traditional MS care. This study was conducted at a nonprofit rehabilitation center. Participants were people with MS who (1) were in a 4-day comprehensive MS program (4Day; n = 24), (2) were receiving care in an MS institute (MSI; n = 10), or (3) were members of an online patient research platform (iConquerMS; iCMS; n = 21). Data were collected at baseline and 1, 6, 12, and 24 months via an electronic portal. They included scores on the Expanded Disability Status Scale, Patient-Determined Disease Steps, MS Impact Scale-29, Multiple Sclerosis Self-Management Scale-Revised, MS Walking Scale-12, Quality of Life in Neurological Disorders, and Spinal Cord Injury Exercise Self-Efficacy Scale. All groups showed improvements across most outcomes at 1 and 6 months. The 4Day and MSI groups had greater gains in self-management, self-efficacy, and quality of life, particularly at 1 month, compared with the iCMS group. Comprehensive MS care, whether delivered intensively over 4 days or through an integrated outpatient program, may enhance self-efficacy and quality of life more effectively than standard care alone. Further research is needed due to small sample sizes, pandemic-related challenges, and limited clinical data for one group.

title: Components of the Support Networks of Multiple Sclerosis Care Partners.
abstract: Care partners support many individuals with multiple sclerosis (MS), but little is known about the support they themselves rely on. This study sought to characterize the support networks used by MS care partners and to identify key characteristics associated with support network size. Fifteen MS care partners completed an online survey. Individual, semistructured interviews captured care partner support network content. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, and correlation coefficients were used to characterize associations between network size and variables of interest. Participants were predominantly women (n = 13, 86.7%) with a mean age of 50.8 (SD = 11.8) years, and reported a median care-recipient Patient-Determined Disease Steps (PDDS) score of 5. Support networks contained a median of 12 different sources of support (range, 8-27). Friends and family members were the most common support sources, reported by 14 (93.3%) and 11 care partners (73.3%), respectively. Next were friends or family of care recipients (n = 9, 60.0%), and the care recipients themselves (n = 9, 60.0%). Only care partner resilience ( Natural supports (ie, friends, family members) were common and important components of care partner support networks. Care recipients were often important members of support networks, highlighting the dyadic disease experience. Findings emphasize the relationship between having support and maintaining resilience among MS care partners. Future efforts to implement novel sources of support must consider existing support networks and the characteristics of individual care partners that are most likely to ensure support uptake and efficacy.

title: Symptoms as Correlates of Health-Related Quality of Life in Black and White Individuals With Multiple Sclerosis.
abstract: Health-related quality of life (HRQOL) is a key health outcome and often compromised in people with multiple sclerosis (MS). Yet the associations between symptoms and HRQOL across racial subgroups remain unclear. To that end, this cross-sectional, comparative study examined symptoms as correlates of HRQOL in Black and White individuals with MS. Black (n = 136) and White (n = 273) individuals with MS completed an online survey assessing walking impairment (12-Item Multiple Sclerosis Walking Scale [MSWS-12]), fatigue (Fatigue Severity Scale [FSS]); depression and anxiety (Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale [HADS-A and HADSD]); and HRQOL (12-Item Short Form Survey Physical and Mental). Bivariate correlations and stepwise linear regression were performed to identify associations between symptoms and HRQOL. MSWS-12, FSS, and HADS-D were significantly associated with physical HRQOL, and HADS-A, HADS-D, and FSS were significantly associated with mental HRQOL within both groups: Black ( Our findings highlight symptoms, including walking impairment, fatigue, anxiety, and depression, as correlates of HRQOL among Black and White individuals with MS and may inform intervention development that targets the symptoms to improve HRQOL across racial groups.

title: Arterial Stiffness Is Higher in People With Multiple Sclerosis Than in Control Group.
abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic, immune-mediated, neurodegenerative disease of the central nervous system with prevalent vascular comorbidities and associated vascular dysfunction involving arterial stiffness. This study examined the difference in arterial stiffness between people with MS and controls and whether the difference was accounted for by anxiety, depression, and walking endurance, variables not usually included in other studies of arterial stiffness in MS. The sample included 129 people with MS (age, 48.5 [10.8] years; 70.5% female; Expanded Disability Status Scale score median, 4) and 51 controls without MS (age, 48.7 [11.3] years; 78.4% female) who completed arterial stiffness, anxiety, and depression assessments and the 6-Minute Walk Test (6MWT). There were significant differences between groups in arterial stiffness ( Our results indicate that people with MS have higher levels of arterial stiffness compared with controls, but this difference is not explained by age, BMI, MAP, anxiety, depression, or walking endurance.

title: Perspectives on End of Life and Medical Assistance in Dying From Saskatchewan People With Multiple Sclerosis.
abstract: Medical assistance in dying (MAID) is a legally available option in Canada. Bill C-14 determined initial eligibility requirements (eg, a patient having a reasonably foreseeable natural death), program safeguards, and a definition of who can assess and administer MAID. Subsequently, Bill C-7 removed the requirement that death must be reasonably foreseeable. Saskatchewan's multiple sclerosis (MS) prevalence rate is among the highest in the world, and some individuals with MS have already accessed MAID. This project explored the perceptions of end of life (EOL) in Saskatchewan, Canada. Using an interpretive description methodology, 22 interviews were conducted with individuals with MS and 5 with key informants for data triangulation. Demographic and symptom severity contextual data, field notes, and reflective interview content were also collected and triangulated. Inductive reflexive thematic analysis was completed. Participants had a mean age of 41.8 years with a wide variability in symptom severity. Their main concerns were retaining self-agency, combating stigma, and leaning into hope and positivity. While valuing decision-making autonomy, they recognized that MS can complicate EOL decision-making. Participants looked to family and health care providers for cues about cognitive changes and found that hope and positivity provided comfort as the disease progressed. Understanding participants' perspectives will help clinicians support individuals as they navigate their disease trajectory during EOL care planning, will help policy makers enhance the health care system to ensure EOL care accessibility for the MS community, and support individual choice for people with MS.

title: Domain-Specific Cognitive Associations With Standing Balance in Multiple Sclerosis.
abstract: Balance impairments and cognitive deficits are both prevalent in individuals with multiple sclerosis (MS) and contribute to elevated fall risk. Although prior studies have examined global cognition and balance, few have investigated the relation between specific cognitive domains and balance performance under progressively challenging static conditions. Fifty-four ambulatory individuals with MS completed 4 standing balance tasks that increased in difficulty by altering visual input (eyes open/closed) and stance (feet apart/together). Sway velocity was measured using inertial sensors. Participants also completed assessments of processing speed (Symbol Digit Modalities Test [SDMT]), attention and cognitive flexibility (Trail Making Test parts A [TMT-A] and B), verbal and visuospatial memory (California Verbal Learning Test, Brief Visuospatial Memory Test-Revised), and concern about falling (Falls Efficacy Scale-International [FES-I]). Spearman correlations and linear regressions, adjusted for age, sex, and disability level, were used to examine associations between cognitive/psychological variables and balance performance. Processing speed (SDMT) was significantly associated with sway during the least complex condition (eyes open, feet apart). Under more challenging conditions (eyes closed), attention (TMT-A) and concern about falling (FES-I) emerged as significant predictors of balance performance. They remained significant after adjusting for disability level. Domain-specific cognitive performance and concern about falling are associated with postural control in people with MS, particularly under sensory-conflicting conditions. These findings highlight the multifactorial nature of balance impairment in MS and suggest that cognitive and psychological assessments may aid in identifying individuals at increased fall risk.

title: Real-World Classification of Pain States in Multiple Sclerosis Patients using Wearable Sensor Data and Ensemble Machine Learning.
abstract: Pain assessment remains challenging due to its subjective nature and reliance on self-reports. These challenges are particularly relevant for multiple sclerosis (MS) patients, for whom pain is among the most common and fluctuating symptoms, occurring in multiple forms. Wearable sensors combined with machine learning (ML) offer the potential for continuous and more objective pain monitoring by leveraging physiological signals in real-world contexts. We monitored 18 MS patients over 48 h using the Empatica E4 wristband to collect photoplethysmography, electrodermal activity, skin temperature, and accelerometer data. Physiological features were extracted from 5-, 10-, and 15-min time windows preceding hourly self-reported pain assessment during waking hours. Univariate associations with pain states were evaluated using linear mixed effects models, correcting for multiple comparisons. For classification purposes, feature selection was performed via recursive feature elimination, and 5 ML algorithms were trained and tested with leave-one-subject-out cross-validation. Model performance was evaluated using the F1 score and the sensitivity-specificity balance. For univariate analysis, after correction, only 2 out of 43 features showed significant differences between pain and no-pain states. For the classification task, models based on 5-min windows generally performed the best. The highest F1 score (0.78) was achieved by a Support Vector Machine using 2 features from 5-min windows, while XGBoost achieved the best sensitivity-specificity balance (0.69/0.68) with 2 features from 15-min windows. Wearable physiological signals may contain information relevant to pain-state classification in people with MS. However, these results should be considered preliminary, requiring validation in larger, independent cohorts to establish the robustness and generalizability of the proposed approach.

title: Rebound-Like Inflammatory Activity Presenting as a Tumefactive Demyelinating Lesion after Teriflunomide Discontinuation: A Case Report.
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Rebound after teriflunomide discontinuation is uncommon and difficult to distinguish from ordinary disease reactivation without a documented pretreatment baseline. Tumefactive demyelination is a rarely reported post-cessation phenotype. CASE PRESENTATION: This report presents a 39-year-old woman with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis had no relapses, Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) worsening, or new MRI lesions during approximately 5 years of teriflunomide treatment. She stopped treatment without medical supervision or an accelerated elimination procedure for pregnancy planning. Four months later, persistent headache prompted MRI, which showed a 2.6 × 2.6-cm right frontal periventricular tumefactive demyelinating lesion with edema, peripheral diffusion restriction, and mild ring enhancement, plus a new left cerebellar plaque. EDSS remained 0. Absolute lymphocyte count rose from 600 cells/μL at the last on-treatment visit to 1,700 cells/μL at presentation. Serum MOG-IgG and AQP4-IgG and CSF cytology were negative; a type 2 oligoclonal-band pattern was present, and targeted infectious screening showed no evidence of active infection. Teriflunomide concentration was <0.02 mg/L twice, 14 days apart. Intravenous methylprednisolone (1 g/day for 5 days) resolved the headache. Cladribine was then started, and 1-month MRI showed marked regression. EDSS remained 0 and no new or enhancing lesion appeared through 12 months. CONCLUSION: The tumor-like lesion exceeded the patient's pretreatment radiological phenotype, but the absence of objective deficit, EDSS worsening, and a high lesion burden makes definitive rebound uncertain. Rebound-like post-cessation inflammatory activity is the most defensible description. Supervised treatment transition and clinical and MRI monitoring are important when teriflunomide is stopped.

title: A semantic digital health pipeline for interpretable and longitudinal gait monitoring using wearable sensors.
abstract: Wearable gait monitoring can support neurological follow-up, but raw inertial time-series are difficult to interpret clinically. To evaluate a semantic pipeline that converts raw wearable streams into structured gait events for free-living monitoring. Instrumented smart socks captured tri-axial accelerometer and gyroscope signals from a bilateral inertial measurement unit (IMU) configuration. Data were stored as raw time-series. A deterministic rule-based pipeline derived time-bounded events (per-limb sensor-reception intervals, concurrent bilateral candidate intervals, per-limb effective-movement intervals, and bilateral gait episodes) in a relational database. The semantic layer was published as a Web Ontology Language (OWL) ontology with an Ontop ontology-based data access (OBDA) mapping and reusable SPARQL Protocol and RDF Query Language (SPARQL) queries. Feasibility was evaluated in 44 participants (31 people with multiple sclerosis (PwMS) and 13 controls) across 257 monitoring sessions. The pipeline identified 6,224 gait episodes (∼60.8 hours walking). Episode counts were right-skewed (mean 141.5 episodes/participant, 95% CI 109-174). Most participants (80%) showed low left-right asymmetry (mean index 0.069, 95% CI 0.040-0.107), while elevated imbalance was concentrated in low-data participants. Against standardised in-clinic tests, positive-interval detection sensitivity was 85% (50/59 intervals with bilateral data) after per-session clock alignment using the same annotations; this potentially optimistic estimate does not establish specificity or free-living false-positive performance. In the frozen analysis snapshot, semantic-consistency checking confirmed that 100% of the 6,224 reported gait episodes were temporally contained within concurrent bilateral candidate intervals (activity_all). Hierarchical semantic temporal events enable transparent, scalable, and interpretable real-world gait monitoring. By releasing the ontology, OBDA mapping, and queries, the pipeline supports longitudinal assessment, limb balance analysis, and interoperable health-system integration. The same approach is applicable beyond gait to other wearable-derived digital biomarkers and rehabilitation-monitoring tasks. This work does not deliver a validated clinical gait assessment tool, but demonstrates reusable digital health representations.

title: Impact of 2024 Revisions of Multiple Sclerosis Diagnostic Criteria in People With Radiologically Isolated Syndrome.
abstract: The biological onset of multiple sclerosis (MS) precedes its clinical onset by years, as shown by MRI and CSF biomarkers. The 2024 revisions of the McDonald criteria extend, for the first time, MS diagnosis to selected cases of radiologically isolated syndrome (RIS), that is, to people with incidentally discovered CNS lesions suggestive of autoimmune inflammatory demyelination, in the absence of typical symptoms. The aim of this multicenter study was to assess the proportion of patients with RIS reclassified as MS, after applying the 2024 criteria. Adult participants (≥18 years) fulfilling the 2023 Lebrun-Frénay RIS criteria were selected from 22 Italian MS tertiary centers. Real-world, registry-based data were retrospectively collected at both baseline and follow-up. Reclassification followed 2024 criteria, allowing a MS diagnosis in RIS cases with ≥1 T2-hyperintense lesion in ≥2 typical MS regions (i.e., dissemination in space [DIS]), plus either MRI evidence of dissemination in time (DIT), CSF positivity, or central vein sign (CVS) positivity. Descriptive statistics were used. Among 236 patients with RIS (mean age 38.9 ± 11.6 years; 70.3% female; median follow-up 3.0 years [interquartile range {IQR}: 1.1-6]), at baseline, 228 (96.6%) fulfilled DIS, 51 (21.6%) fulfilled radiologic DIT, and 152 of 201 individuals with available CSF data were CSF-positive (75.6%). CVS data were available for 5 of 236 individuals; none were CVS-positive. At baseline, the 2024 criteria resulted in a MS diagnosis in 159 of 236 patients with RIS (67.4%). Of 42 patients with RIS experiencing a clinical event during follow-up, 88.1% would have been reclassified as MS a median of 2 years earlier (IQR: 1.0-5.5). During follow-up, 18 of 236 additional participants (7.6%) met the diagnostic criteria through radiologic DIT. The introduction of the 2024 criteria results in an earlier diagnosis of MS, before clinical manifestations of focal CNS damage, in most people formerly classified as RIS. Study limitations include incomplete kappa free light chain index data and nonstandardized MRI acquisition protocols; particularly, retrospective CVS assessment was negligible in this real-life context. Future studies including the full spectrum of asymptomatic individuals with MRI abnormalities and available paraclinical diagnostic tools are needed to better define the impact of 2024 revised criteria in this population.

title: Toward a Biology-Driven Diagnosis of Multiple Sclerosis: What the 2024 McDonald Criteria Mean for Radiologically Isolated Syndrome.
Occupational Exposure to Petroleum-Derived Lubricants and Risk of Multiple Sclerosis.
abstract: Lung irritants such as smoking and organic solvents are established risk factors of multiple sclerosis (MS), with effects influenced by genetic susceptibility, particularly leukocyte antigen (HLA) This investigation was based on a Swedish population-based case-control design. Incident MS cases were consecutively recruited by neurologists at 40 clinics (2005-2015). Inclusion criteria comprised residence in Sweden, age 16-70 years, and a diagnosis of MS confirmed by a neurologist according to the McDonald criteria. Controls were randomly selected from the national population register using density sampling and frequency-matched to cases by age, sex, and residential area. Exposure to petroleum-derived lubricants was assessed using questionnaire data. Logistic regression was used to estimate odds ratios (ORs) and 95% CIs for MS in relation to occupational exposure to petroleum-derived lubricants. Interactions with smoking, The study population comprised 2,872 incident MS cases and 6,122 controls (mean age: 34.6 years; 72% female). Occupational exposure to petroleum-derived lubricants was associated with increased MS risk (OR 1.38, 95% CI 1.16-1.65), with a modest exposure-duration response. The association persisted when applying a 7-year exposure lag (OR 1.55, 95% CI 1.27-1.90). A positive interaction was identified between petroleum exposure and smoking (AP 0.34, 95% CI 0.10-0.55). Among the subset with available HLA data (2,070 cases and 2,899 controls), petroleum exposure interacted with the absence of Occupational exposure to petroleum-derived lubricants was associated with MS risk, with stronger associations among smokers and participants with established genetic susceptibility. These findings add to the evidence that lung irritants and gene-environment interactions contribute to MS susceptibility but require replication in independent populations.

title: Timing Is Everything: Occupational Petrolatum-Based Lubricant Exposure and Multiple Sclerosis.
Physical and psychological burden in RRMS: depression and fatigue beyond disease duration.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic, autoimmune, demyelinating and neurodegenerative disease. Accumulation of physical and psychological disabilities adversely affects patients' health-related quality of life. The 29-item Multiple Sclerosis Impact Scale (MSIS-29) is a self-reported measure of the physical and psychological burden. OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the physical and psychological impact levels in patients with MS and to examine their relationship with disease duration. METHODS: We enrolled 100 consecutive adults aged 18 to 55 years with relapsing-remitting MS (RRMS). The Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS), annual relapse rate (ARR), Beck Depression Inventory (BDI), Fatigue Severity Scale (FSS), MSIS-29, and Timed 25-Foot Walk Test (25-FWT) were applied. RESULTS: A total of 57 participants (57%) were female patients. The mean age was 38.5 ± 8.0 years, and the mean disease duration, 9.8 ± 6.8 years. The mean MSIS-29 physical and psychological scores were 36.7 ± 15.7 and 45.3 ± 20.4 respectively. No significant differences were found between patients with disease duration ≤ 10 and > 10 years in terms of the physical (p = 0.263) or psychological (p = 0.551) subscales. Physical impact was significantly associated with the female sex (p = 0.021) and the scpres on the EDSS (p = 0.030), BDI (p < 0.001), and FSS (p < 0.001). Psychological impact showed significant associations with the female sex (p = 0.005), ARR (p = 0.020), and the scores on the BDI (p < 0.001), and FSS (p < 0.001). On multivariate regression, the scores on the EDSS, BDI, and 25-FWT were independent predictors of physical impact, while the female sex and the scores on the EDSS and BDI were independent predictors of psychological impact. CONCLUSION: Disease duration did not predict physical or psychological impact in RRMS. Depression severity, lower-extremity function, and the female sex were the independent determinants of disease-related impact in the multivariate analysis. The association of fatigue with disease impact, significant at the bivariate level, was attenuated by depression in the multivariate analysis. Routine assessment of these modifiable factors should be accompanied by disease-modifying treatments in MS care.

title: Menopause and Neurology: Clinical Essentials.
abstract: PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Menopause is a neurobiological transition with important implications for neurologic care. This review summarizes the physiology and hormonal changes of spontaneous menopause and its treatment as applied to cognition, epilepsy, migraine, multiple sclerosis (MS), and stroke. It aims to serve as a resource for neurologists when managing patients in this transitional life stage. RECENT FINDINGS: Hormonal shifts associated with menopause, particularly declining estrogen and fluctuating estrogen-to-progesterone ratios, influence symptoms, disease expression, and treatment across multiple neurologic conditions. Perimenopause is often associated with subjective cognitive complaints, in part attributed to hypoestrogenism, along with secondary effects from sleep disturbance, vasomotor symptoms, and mood changes. Cognitive symptoms are often transient and rarely with objective neuropsychological deficits or progression. In epilepsy, menopause-related endogenous and exogenous hormones may influence seizure susceptibility and alter antiseizure medication metabolism. Migraine may worsen during perimenopause, especially in estrogen-sensitive phenotypes, with postmenopause stabilization once hormones plateau. In MS, perimenopause and postmenopause contribute to overlapping age-related and MS-related symptoms and is a period of high clinical need with potential acceleration in disability progression despite reduced relapse rate. Ischemic stroke risk rises sharply in postmenopausal women driven by advancing age, accumulation of cardiometabolic risk, and loss of estrogen's protective effects. Oral estrogen-containing systemic menopause hormone therapy (MHT) is associated with increased thromboembolic events (including stroke), whereas transdermal regimens seem safer and are preferred at low or standard doses (≤50 mcg estradiol patch or ≤1.5 mg [or 2 pumps] per day of 0.06% estradiol gel). Timing of initiation also modulates this risk and plays a critical role with a favorable risk:benefit window when initiated in women younger than 60 years or within 10 years of menopause onset. SUMMARY: Neurologists should routinely consider reproductive history, menopausal stage, symptom burden, and disease risk factors when evaluating midlife and older female patients. When appropriately selected, MHT can be safely used in many neurologic populations, with nonoral routes for estrogen and nonhormonal options generally preferred. Incorporating menopausal considerations into neurologic practice offers an important opportunity to optimize care and advance precision medicine.

title: The impact of rising global temperatures on neurological diseases.
abstract: Climate change, driven predominantly by anthropogenic actions, represents a defining challenge of the 21st century. While its general health implications are well documented, the specific impact of global warming on neurological diseases has remained underemphasized for decades. To evaluate the association between rising global temperatures and the exacerbation or incidence of various neurological conditions through a systematic review. A systematic search was conducted in the PubMed/MEDLINE and SciELO databases for studies published between 2011 and 2026. Following strict eligibility criteria, 13 peer-reviewed articles were selected for qualitative synthesis. The evidence reveals that rising temperatures are increasingly linked to the worsening of conditions such as epilepsy, stroke, multiple sclerosis (MS), and neurodegenerative disorders like Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases. Specifically, heat exposure is associated with higher hospitalization rates and acute symptom exacerbation, such as Uhthoff's phenomenon in MS and autonomic thermoregulatory failure in Parkinson's. Although some geographic and methodological discrepancies exist, particularly regarding stroke and seizure frequency, the overall trend indicates increased neurological vulnerability to thermal stress. While research is expanding, neurological diseases remain an understudied frontier of the climate crisis. Targeted scientific investigation and robust public health strategies are imperative to mitigate the emerging neurological risks of a warming planet.

title: Cryptic Presentations of Neurologic Wilson Disease With ATP7B Peptide Assessments.
abstract: To illustrate the phenotypic variability in neurologic Wilson disease (NWD) and diagnostic value of ATP7B peptide testing in resolving WD cases. We conducted a case series analysis of 3 individuals with suspected NWD. Clinical presentation, diagnostic workup including traditional biomarkers, genetic testing, and ATP7B peptide quantification by immuno-selected reaction monitoring mass spectrometry were reviewed. The 3 patients demonstrated diverse neurologic presentations: (1) an adult with coexisting Parkinson disease and WD, exhibiting parkinsonian features with partial response to dopaminergic therapy; (2) a child with early-onset dystonia and neuropsychiatric symptoms; and (3) an adult initially misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis. In these cases, ATP7B peptide testing revealed either markedly reduced or undetectable levels, confirming WD. These cases emphasize the diagnostic complexity of NWD. ATP7B peptide analysis via immuno-SRM-MS provided direct evidence of ATP7B protein deficiency and confirmed variant pathogenicity demonstrating its use as a rapid, noninvasive, functionally informative diagnostic adjunct. As the assay is further validated and piloted for newborn screening, it holds promise for improving early detection and clinical outcomes in WD.

title: Th17 cells and neutrophils: exploiting their crosstalk for multiple sclerosis therapeutics.
abstract: Substantial evidence from human studies and experimental mouse models highlights a key role for dysregulated Th17 cell responses in the pathogenesis of chronic inflammatory disorders, including neuroinflammatory conditions such as multiple sclerosis (MS). Th17 cell biology is closely linked to neutrophils, with Th17 cells promoting optimal neutrophil effector functions and conversely, neutrophils propagating Th17 responses, indicating bi-directional Th17 neutrophil crosstalk is necessary for optimal type 17 immunity. Importantly, recent studies demonstrate communication networks between neutrophils and Th17 cell responses in numerous chronic inflammatory disorders suggesting that dysregulation of this interplay contributes to disease pathogenesis. This review discusses the current understanding of Th17-neutrophil bi-directional crosstalk and focusses specifically on how dysregulation of this interplay may drive chronic inflammation during central nervous system (CNS) autoimmunity. Furthermore, we consider how evolving therapeutics could exploit these interactions for the development of new treatment strategies.

title: Associations between different types of chronic lesions and gray matter atrophy in multiple sclerosis.
abstract: Focal lesions are one of the key factors contributing to brain atrophy in multiple sclerosis (MS) patients. This study aimed to investigate the associations between the different types of chronic lesions and gray matter atrophy in MS patients. The study recruited MS patients from two institutions, along with healthy controls (HCs). Lesions were classified into paramagnetic rim lesions (PRLs) and non-PRLs. Lesion volume, diffusion kurtosis imaging (DKI) parameters, brain volume (BV), gray matter volume (GMV), and cortical thickness (CT) were extracted. Differences between PRLs and non-PRLs, as well as between MS and HC groups, were analyzed. The associations between lesions and brain structure features were assessed using a general linear model. The study included 46 relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS) patients and 31 HCs. A total of 940 chronic lesions were collected, of which 382 were PRLs (41%) and the remainder were non-PRLs. PRLs had larger volume and lower DKI parameters compared to non-PRLs. The MS group showed reduced GMV and CT compared to the HC group. The volume of all lesion types was negatively correlated with brain structure features, while some DKI parameters showed positive correlations. The Kr value of non-PRLs, the Kr value of whole lesions, and the volume of whole lesions were most strongly correlated with GMV, BV, and CT, respectively. Both the volume and microstructural damage of chronic MS lesions are associated with gray matter atrophy. Contrary to expectations, the microstructural impairment of non-PRLs showed a stronger association with atrophy than that of the more destructive PRLs. This highlights the need to pay more attention to the role of non-PRLs in disease progression.

title: Noncanonical Signaling Network of Nogo-A: A New Perspective on Multi-target Regulation, Neuroplasticity, and Disease Intervention Beyond NgR.
abstract: The membrane protein Nogo-A, initially identified for its inhibitory role in axonal regeneration through the Nogo receptor (NgR), is now recognized as a central hub in a complex noncanonical signaling network. Recent evidence indicates that Nogo-A engages diverse receptors and intracellular pathways beyond NgR to modulate neuroplasticity, synaptic stability, and glial function. This multi-target regulatory capacity characterizes Nogo-A as a critical determinant of neural repair and degeneration, with implications for conditions such as spinal cord injury, multiple sclerosis, and Alzheimer's disease. Noncanonical Nogo-A signaling intersects with growth factor cascades, inflammatory responses, and cytoskeletal dynamics, offering novel therapeutic targets for neural repair. This review synthesizes current knowledge on alternative Nogo-A signaling mechanisms and highlights their potential to redefine strategies for neuroregeneration and disease intervention.

title: Mitochondrial Haplogroup U and multiple sclerosis risk in Arab and Near Eastern populations: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: Multiple Sclerosis (MS) is an inflammatory neurodegenerative disease with incompletely understood aetiology beyond the HLA-DRB1 locus. Mitochondrial haplogroup U, prevalent in Middle Eastern and Near Eastern populations, encodes functional variants in NADH dehydrogenase subunits associated with elevated reactive oxygen species (ROS) production. A 2022 study (Al-Kafaji et al., PLoS ONE) reported a nominal association between haplogroup U and RRMS in Saudi Arab patients (OR 6.26; 95% CI 0.82-48.10) in a single, small (n = 47) cohort. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to determine whether this signal is supported by independently verifiable case-control data from other Arab or Near Eastern populations. PRISMA 2020 systematic review. PubMed/MEDLINE was searched to 15 July 2026 using a concept-level strategy - ("mitochondrial DNA"[tiab] OR "mtDNA"[tiab] OR "DNA, Mitochondrial"[MeSH] OR "Mitochondria"[MeSH]) AND ("haplogroup"[tiab] OR "haplogroups"[tiab] OR "haplotype"[tiab]) AND ("multiple sclerosis"[tiab] OR "Multiple Sclerosis"[MeSH] OR "demyelinating"[tiab] OR "RRMS"[tiab]) - with no population terms applied at the search stage; population eligibility (Arab or Near Eastern cohort) was assessed during screening rather than baked into the search string, to maximise sensitivity. Eligible studies were case-control studies reporting mitochondrial haplogroup U frequency in MS cases versus healthy controls in an Arab or Near Eastern population, with data sufficient to construct a 2 × 2 table. Odds ratios were pooled using a fixed-effect inverse-variance model. The search identified 30 records. After screening and full-text assessment, two studies met full inclusion criteria for quantitative pooling: Al-Kafaji et al. [1] (Saudi Arabia, n = 47) and Hassani-Kumleh et al. [2] (Iran, n = 154); total pooled N = 201 (77 MS cases, 124 controls). The fixed-effect pooled OR was 4.11 (95% CI 1.25-13.55; p = 0.020), with no meaningful heterogeneity (I²=0%, Cochran's Q = 0.25, df = 1). Two further Near Eastern studies (Houshmand et al. [3]; Ghabaee et al. [4]) reported related but non-poolable data - haplogroup J association and a haplogroup U case-series prevalence without a control arm, respectively - and are discussed narratively. Across two independently verified Near Eastern case-control cohorts, mitochondrial haplogroup U is significantly associated with increased MS risk (pooled OR 4.11, 95% CI 1.25-13.55). The evidence base remains small, and the wide confidence interval reflects this. A larger, prospective, adequately powered study in Arab and Near Eastern MS cohorts is needed to confirm and refine this association.

title: Direct medical costs of chronic diseases in Jordan: a systematic review.
abstract: Chronic diseases are a leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, with prevalence rising because of lifestyle factors and increasing life expectancy. In developing countries, including Jordan, these conditions pose growing health and economic burdens. This systematic review assessed available literature on the economic burden of chronic diseases in Jordan. Following PRISMA guidelines, we searched Medline PubMed, Embase, PubMed Central, and Scopus, supplemented by Google/Google Scholar and reference lists, for studies reporting direct medical costs of chronic diseases in Jordan. Titles, abstracts, and full texts were screened independently by two reviewers. Study characteristics and mean annual per-patient costs were extracted and verified. Costs were standardized to per-patient, per-year estimates in 2025 USD, including outpatient, inpatient, diagnostic, emergency, and medication expenses. The quality of included studies was assessed using the adapted version of Drummond checklist for economic studies. Database search identified 147 records. After removal of one duplicate record, 146 records were screened, and 19 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility. Ultimately, eleven studies were included. They reported costs for cancers, diabetic retinopathy, severe renal disease, thalassaemia, paediatric asthma, and multiple sclerosis, mostly using retrospective designs. Mean annual costs ranged from $35 to $30,567 (2025 USD), and the greatest costs were for end-stage renal disease. Of cancer studied, breast cancer and colorectal cancer were associated with substantial annual direct medical costs, although estimates varied considerably between studies because of differences in disease populations, data sources, and cost methodologies. The mean annual cost for all conditions was $10,035 (2025 USD). When weighted against the sample sizes, the pooled mean cost was $6,914 USD. The overall quality of included studies was judged to be moderate, with most studies clearly defining study populations, disease conditions, and data sources used for cost estimation. Chronic kidney disease, breast cancer, and multiple sclerosis imposed substantial medical costs in Jordan. Evidence for other major conditions was limited, highlighting the need for further research to guide health care planning, resource allocation, and cost-effective chronic disease management.

title: Microglia drive demyelination via multiple sclerosis antibodies and BTK signaling.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Microglia are the predominant immune cells in multiple sclerosis (MS) demyelinating lesions, where they phagocytose myelin, but whether they destroy myelin or merely scavenge its debris is unknown. Here, we explore whether pathogenic autoantibodies found in MS may induce the phagocytic destruction of myelin by microglia. title: Assessing the clinical- and cost-effectiveness of REFUEL-MS, a digital therapeutic for multiple sclerosis-related fatigue: study protocol for a randomised controlled trial.
abstract: Fatigue is a common and disabling symptom affecting up to 90% of people living with multiple sclerosis (MS). Cognitive-behavioural, exercise and balance interventions are effective in reducing MS fatigue, but there is currently no standardised, accessible treatment in the UK healthcare system. REFUEL-MS is an app-based, healthcare professional (HCP)-supported intervention designed to reduce MS fatigue using cognitive-behavioural, exercise and balance principles. This trial aims to test the efficacy, safety and cost-effectiveness of REFUEL-MS compared to treatment as usual. This is a two-arm, parallel-group superiority randomised controlled trial. Adults with confirmed MS, who experience fatigue (scoring > 4 on the Chalder Fatigue Questionnaire [CFQ]), and are not on a new disease-modifying treatment (< 6 months) will be eligible. Participants will be recruited across the UK via the UK MS Register, NHS clinics, and community networks/organisations. Participants will be randomised 1:1 at the individual level using a centralised web-based system, stratified by MS type and recruitment source, to receive the REFUEL-MS intervention or treatment as usual. Participants receiving REFUEL-MS will complete weekly app sessions and four online HCP appointments over 16 weeks. All participants will complete online assessments at baseline, and 4, 6 and 12 months post-randomisation. Participants and HCPs will be unblinded, while the outcome assessors and senior statistician will be blinded. The primary outcome is fatigue severity (CFQ) at 6 months post-randomisation. Secondary outcomes include fatigue impact and improvement, mood, quality of life, service use, physical activity, and adverse events, assessed at multiple timepoints. The target sample is 378 to detect a minimal clinically important difference on the CFQ between groups. Safety and cost-effectiveness will also be evaluated and interviews will be conducted with a subset of participants to explore user and healthcare professionals' experiences with the intervention. If effective and safe, REFUEL-MS has the potential to be a scalable intervention. Implementation will be tested in a real-world multiple-case study following this trial. The trial was pre-registered on the UK's Clinical Study Registry on 20/06/2025 (ISRCTN82686286; https://doi.org/10.1186/ISRCTN82686286 ).

title: Converging pathomechanisms link SARS-CoV-2 infection with major neurodegenerative diseases.
authors: on the behalf of WP4, the COMMUTE Consortium
abstract: Neurological complications are among typical clinical manifestations, both during the acute phase of SARS-CoV-2 infection and long-term post-acute COVID-19 sequelae, i.e., Long COVID. A growing body of evidence connects SARS-CoV-2 infection to systemic inflammation, peripheral immune dysregulation, functional alteration of the blood-brain barrier (BBB), neuroinflammatory processes, mitochondrial dysfunction and pathological protein aggregation, all of which are central to the pathogenesis of major neurodegenerative diseases. In this review, we discuss the converging shared underlying molecular mechanisms that link the 'acute' SARS-CoV-2 infection that often only lasts for days and 'chronic' neurodegenerative diseases that often take decades to develop. We further review human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs)-derived brain organoid and BBB models for Parkinson's disease (PD) and Alzheimer's disease (AD) as well as artificial intelligence (AI)-facilitated knowledge graph methods that are used to hypothesize and validate the potential mechanistic links. We propose that besides the established links between viral infections and neurodegenerative or neuroinflammatory conditions, such as Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) in multiple sclerosis or herpes zoster in AD, SARS-CoV-2 infection might be another important factor driving the future burden of the most common neurodegenerative diseases.

title: Advanced age at onset is associated with distinct functional brain reorganization in multiple sclerosis.
abstract: Functional network reorganization supports compensatory mechanisms in multiple sclerosis, but ageing and later disease onset may alter this balance. Late-onset multiple sclerosis (age at onset ≥50 years) represents a relevant subgroup to examine how disease onset in older age is associated with functional connectivity abnormalities. In this cross-sectional study, we investigated resting-state functional connectivity alterations in late-onset multiple sclerosis versus adult-onset multiple sclerosis and their associations with clinical, cognitive and structural MRI measures. Thirty-four late-onset multiple sclerosis, 169 sex- and disease duration-matched adult-onset multiple sclerosis, and 163 age- and sex-matched healthy controls underwent clinical, neuropsychological (Brief Repeatable Battery of Neuropsychological Tests) and MRI assessment including resting-state functional MRI. Independent component analysis quantified resting-state functional connectivity within 10 large-scale networks. Between-group differences were tested using sex- and scanner-adjusted voxel-wise models (

title: An ARG1-associated immunometabolic program in bone marrow PMN-MDSC-like cells in multiple sclerosis and experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis.
abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic inflammatory demyelinating disease of the central nervous system. Recent work indicates that bone-marrow hematopoietic niches sense CNS autoimmunity and enhance myeloid output. However, whether MS bone marrow contains an immunometabolic PMN-MDSC-like state, and whether related ARG1-associated observations can be examined in a cross-species EAE context, remains unclear. We reanalyzed single-cell RNA sequencing data from treatment-naive patients with MS and healthy controls, focusing on myeloid states. We used donor-aware proportion analysis, trajectory inference, module scoring, donor-pseudobulk pathway enrichment, expression-based transcription-factor prioritization, co-expression analysis, ligand-target inference, and ARG1 virtual perturbation. We also quantified flow-gated bone marrow PMN-MDSCs and ARG1 protein in MOG35-55-induced EAE and tested systemic prophylactic oral nor-NOHA. MS bone marrow showed myeloid skewing and a heterogeneous PMN-MDSC-like transcriptional state, while donor-level subtype proportions were comparable between groups. Neutrophil degranulation showed the strongest BH-supported donor-pseudobulk enrichment, and expression-based regulatory and communication analyses converged on an ARG1-associated network. In EAE, flow-gated bone-marrow PMN-MDSCs and ARG1 protein were increased, and systemic prophylactic nor-NOHA was associated with lower clinical scores and reduced spinal-cord pathology. These data identify an ARG1-associated immunometabolic program in bone-marrow PMN-MDSC-like cells and connect the human transcriptional landscape with ARG1 protein expression and pharmacologic responses in EAE. Together, the findings establish ARG1-associated immunometabolism as a focused pathway for mechanistic and translational investigation.

title: Grey matter atrophy signatures and their genetic associations: a trans-disease study of Alzheimer's disease and multiple sclerosis.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) and multiple sclerosis (MS) share neuroimmune mechanisms that drive neurodegeneration. Current clinical interventions are largely confined to a single-disease approach, owing to the absence of trans-disease diagnostic markers and common therapeutic targets. To map common and disease-specific grey matter (GM) atrophy patterns in AD and MS and identify their genetic correlations. We performed a trans-disease meta-analysis in large-sample neuroimaging data from 2001 to 2024 (2,070 MS versus 1,625 healthy control, and 1,624 AD versus 1,607 healthy control) to map GM atrophy regions. The cross-sample partial least squares regression was applied to integrate gene expression profiles from the Allen Human Brain Atlas with region-specific GM atrophy patterns, achieving cross-scale analysis of identify neurodegeneration-associated genes. MS-specific atrophy localized to the bilateral dorsomedial thalamic nucleus and precentral gyrus, whereas AD-specific atrophy centered on bilateral hippocampus-amygdala complex in age-unadjusted comparisons. The common atrophy patterns were found in the bilateral superior temporal gyrus, insulae, posterior cingulate cortex, amygdalae, and striatal components. We identified 834 genes whose spatial expression patterns were associated with the common GM atrophy pattern in AD and MS, including PLS2 + and PLS2- subsets, which encompass biological processes such as immunological homeostasis imbalance, cellular stress response, and neurometabolic/functional regulation. Findings establish shared cortical-limbic-striatal atrophy as pivotal neurodegeneration nexus in AD and MS. The identified gene-imaging signatures provide insights into potential pathway-specific mechanisms and may inform future therapeutic target discovery for dual-disease intervention.

title: Combining pharmacological and non-invasive brain stimulation strategies to promote remyelination in multiple sclerosis.
abstract: Remyelination in multiple sclerosis (MS) fails for several, partly overlapping reasons. The differentiation of oligodendrocyte precursor cells into myelin-producing oligodendrocytes is impaired both by intrinsic factors and by the surrounding lesion environment, which becomes increasingly inflammatory and senescent with age. Pharmacological strategies acting on a single target to promote oligodendrocyte lineage progression have been successful in animal models but have yet to produce meaningful clinical benefit in people with MS (pwMS). In this perspective paper, we argue that simultaneously targeting several of the mechanisms underlying this failure is a more promising route to repairing myelin lesions in pwMS. We outline how non-invasive brain stimulation (NIBS) might be leveraged to shift the glial microenvironment towards a pro-regenerative, remyelinating state, and how this can be paired with targeted pharmacological agents that enhance oligodendrocyte differentiation. We also discuss how the expected effect of such a combination may depend on age and lesion stage. This framework may offer a rational route beyond the translational failures of single-target remyelination therapies.

title: Neuron myelination is accelerated by Bruton's tyrosine kinase inhibition via microglial extracellular vesicles.
abstract: The altered myelin repair observed in demyelinating diseases such as multiple sclerosis (MS) potentially exposes axons to various stressors, with consequent neurodegeneration. Preclinical evidence has demonstrated that Bruton's tyrosine kinase inhibitors (BTKi), such as ibrutinib, delay MS progression by acting on myeloid cells. We investigated the effects of ibrutinib on remyelination using a novel in vitro model of spinal cord neurons derived from postnatal mice. We demonstrated that (1) spinal cord neuron cells represent a suitable model for investigating myelination following L‑α‑lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC) treatment; (2) ibrutinib induces remyelination and reduces stathmin‑1 expression in spinal cord cultures; and (3) ibrutinib reduces the inflammatory phenotype of microglia‑like BV2 cells, thereby modulating the expression of miR‑223 in extracellular vesicles (EVs). Altogether, these data pave the way for a better understanding of the mechanisms underlying remyelination following ibrutinib treatment and support the hypothesis that EV‑derived microglial cells play a key role.

title: Altered network organization with shift to local processing during adaptive behaviour in multiple sclerosis.
abstract: To adjust to changing environmental demands, the brain needs to organize and (re)configure mental resources in so-called task sets. Following a network perspective of cognitive functions, these processes are considered to rely on dynamic exchange of information between distant brain regions, possibly synchronized by slow-wave theta oscillations. However, few attempts have been made to describe the directional transfer of information in theta networks during behavioural adaptation. In the current study, we examined directed neural information transfer in 57 healthy individuals and 57 patients with multiple sclerosis with a focus on brain-behaviour associations during task switching. For this, we calculated behavioural switch costs and further applied an artificial neural network-based approach on neurophysiological EEG data to estimate linear and non-linear effective connectivity measures within cortical networks during task switching. Source reconstruction and connectivity analyses revealed distinct neural network architectures and communication strategies during task switching in healthy controls compared to patients with multiple sclerosis. In healthy controls, enhanced modulations of long-range fronto-parietal connectivities were associated with higher reaction time switch costs, possibly reflecting increased cognitive demands rather than adaptive processes. In contrast, patients with multiple sclerosis relied more strongly on local intra-regional modulations, which is consistent with the idea of a dysconnectivity syndrome in multiple sclerosis. Strikingly, stronger modulations in self-connectivities were associated with better accuracy measures in patients with multiple sclerosis, suggesting a compensatory mechanism to support performance. Notably, only non-linear directed connectivity measures were related to behavioural switch costs, emphasizing the importance of non-linear models for adaptive cognitive processes.

title: A 2-year multimodal prospective cohort study to predict sustained progression independent of relapse activity in multiple sclerosis.
abstract: Disability accrual in multiple sclerosis (MS) is heterogeneous. We assessed whether a 2-year multimodal evaluation could identify patients who were developing progression independent of relapse activity (PIRA) or relapse-associated worsening (RAW). Among the 81 MS patients with a 2-year follow-up and outcomes determined through 5 years, a composite for PIRA was developed using Firth's penalized logistic regression analysis; discrimination was calculated as the area under the curve (AUC) using repeated stratified nested cross-validation. In total, 21 patients (25.9%) met the PIRA criteria, 9 (11.1%) met the RAW criteria, and 1 met both criteria. A multivariate Firth regression analysis selected two variables associated with PIRA after adjustment: Modified Fatigue Impact Scale (MFIS) total score (OR 2.04, 95% CI 1.17-3.83; A two-year multimodal assessment identified a biologically coherent PIRA composite driven by intrathecal neuroinflammation and fatigue. No reliable RAW predictor was found, and external validation is warranted.

title: Altered metabolism and endoplasmic reticulum-mitochondria contacts in multiple sclerosis neurons.
abstract: Genetic factors are estimated to account for approximately 30-50% of the risk for developing Multiple sclerosis (MS). Distinct mitochondrial variants, impairments in the respiratory chain, and mitochondrial dysfunction have been reported in individuals affected by MS. Mitochondria and the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) form membrane contact sites (ERMCs) that control important biological functions. Dysregulated ERMCs have been associated with a number of severe consequences for homeostasis, including altered mitochondrial calcium levels, impaired ATP production and abnormal lipid transfer. All of these mechanisms are thought to play an important role in the pathogenesis and disease progression of MS. Here, we investigated the hypothesis that the mitochondrial predisposition plays a crucial role in contributing to MS development. Mitochondrial functionality was analyzed in a model of human induced primary neurons (iPNs), and neuronal precursor cells (NPCs), differentiated from induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) from people with MS and healthy controls (HCs). Seahorse analysis was performed for investigation of the bioenergetic profile of the cells. ERMC and mitochondrial morphological analysis were carried out to investigate the potential impact of mitochondrial dysfunction in MS-derived neurons. Seahorse analysis revealed significant differences in the respiratory complexes (spare capacity: Our data are highlighting the importance of genetic mitochondrial contribution to MS pathology, by showing that MS-derived NPCs and iPNs exhibit altered mitochondrial behavior and morphology compared to healthy control (HC)-derived cells.

title: Fifteen-year real-world pharmacovigilance of multiple sclerosis disease-modifying therapies: adverse event profiles, drug-specific safety signals and clinical implications.
abstract: Disease-modifying therapies (DMTs) are the cornerstone of remission-phase management for multiple sclerosis (MS), a prevalent autoimmune neuroinflammatory disorder of the central nervous system. However, their immune-modulating mechanisms carry inherent risks of systemic and neurological adverse events (ADEs), which remain a major barrier to optimal long-term care. This study aimed to comprehensively characterize the real-world safety profiles of all major MS DMT classes and identify clinically actionable safety signals. We analyzed 15-year (2009Q1-2023Q4) ADE reports for 8 classes of FDA-approved MS DMTs from the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) database. Four disproportionality algorithms (ROR, PRR, BCPNN, MGPS) were used for signal detection. Time-to-onset (TTO) analysis with Weibull distribution and multivariate logistic regression were performed to assess temporal risk patterns and patient-specific risk factors for important medical events (IMEs). A total of 498,847 ADE reports (1,048,575 events) were included, with nearly 50% involving IMEs. The most common ADEs were systemic symptoms, infections, liver injury and alopecia. Notably, progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML, ROR = 15.59) and spontaneous abortion (ROR = 2.54) were identified as high-risk severe events. Drug-specific analysis revealed distinct safety signatures: anti-CD20 antibodies carried the highest infection risk, natalizumab was strongly associated with PML (ROR = 45.62), and teriflunomide had the highest alopecia risk (ROR = 12.73). Approximately 70% of IMEs occurred within 2 years of treatment initiation. Multivariate analysis identified older age, male sex and longer treatment duration as independent risk factors for IMEs, while obesity was a protective factor. This long-term FAERS-based analysis identified potential safety signals associated with major MS DMTs, providing hypothesis-generating evidence to support clinical vigilance and prioritize further validation, but not to estimate incidence, comparative risk, or causality.

title: Non-PML neuroinvasive infections reported with multiple sclerosis disease-modifying therapies: a mechanism-based pharmacovigilance study, 2004-2025.
abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) disease-modifying therapies (DMTs) alter host immunity and may produce pathogen-specific susceptibility to neuroinvasive infection. Comparative evidence is limited because events are rare and postmarketing research focuses mainly on progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML). We analyzed deduplicated US FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) reports from 2004Q1 to 2025Q4 using a prespecified case-non-case design. Tier A comprised direct high-certainty non-PML neuroinvasive infection terms. Tier B comprised a possible CNS infectious syndrome plus pathogen evidence elsewhere in the report, without CNS confirmation; tier A+B was a lower-certainty expanded endpoint for sensitivity and pathogen composition analyses. We estimated overall reporting (E1), pathogen composition within tier A+B (E2), and same-pathogen CNS localization (E3). Five DMT mechanisms were compared with contemporaneous active DMTs using calendar-year Mantel-Haenszel reporting odds ratios and covariate-adjusted Jeffreys-prior penalized logistic models. Among 492,514 reports, 675 were tier A and 82 additional reports were tier B. Tier A aRORs (95% CIs) were 0.82 (0.63-1.05) for anti-CD20 therapies, 1.77 (1.44-2.16) for S1P modulators, 1.32 (1.06-1.64) for natalizumab, 3.28 (2.24-4.66) for alemtuzumab, and 0.56 (0.21-1.19) for cladribine. Fingolimod accounted for 145 of 152 S1P cases and had an aROR of 2.15 (1.75-2.64). Among four mechanisms eligible for E2, pathogen composition differed (LRT 210.59, 9 E1 contrasts were interpreted as separate reporting comparisons, not a formal equality test across mechanisms. S1P reporting was largely fingolimod-driven, and natalizumab-HSV/VZV was the only prespecified pair with adjusted same-pathogen CNS enrichment. Findings support targeted vigilance and confirmatory studies but do not estimate incidence or establish causality.

title: Seizures and epilepsy in MOG antibody-associated disease: from cortical neuroimmunology to clinical practice.
abstract: Myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody-associated disease (MOGAD) is an inflammatory demyelinating disorder distinct from multiple sclerosis (MS) and aquaporin-4-IgG-positive neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (AQP4-NMOSD). Seizures are an important but incompletely characterized manifestation. Their reported prevalence is strongly age-dependent-approximately 30% in pediatric-onset versus 7% in adult-onset cohorts, although these estimates are influenced by referral and publication bias-and clusters around cerebral cortical encephalitis (CCE) and FLAIR-hyperintense lesions in anti-MOG-associated encephalitis with seizures (FLAMES). This raises a mechanistic question: why is cortical MOGAD particularly ictogenic, and how does demyelination interact with lesion anatomy and inflammatory composition to promote cortical hyperexcitability? This review places the neuroimmunology of MOGAD-related seizures at its center. We summarize the epidemiology, age gradient and clinical spectrum-CCE/FLAMES, acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM)-associated seizures, isolated sentinel seizures, status epilepticus, new-onset refractory status epilepticus (NORSE), and MOG-N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDAR) overlap-together with the distinction between acute symptomatic seizures and autoimmune-associated epilepsy. We then examine MOG-IgG effector biology, the CD4+ T-cell- and macrophage-predominant pathology, B-cell compartmentalization, the meningo-cortical axis, and the Th17/interleukin-6-weighted cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) milieu.
