Candidate downstream pathways of inflammatory ictogenesis are presented with an explicit separation between MOGAD-specific associations and mechanisms extrapolated from epilepsy. Finally, we translate this framework into differential diagnosis, assay interpretation, electroencephalographic evaluation, immunotherapy-first management, antiseizure medication (ASM) review, neuropsychological follow-up and testable research priorities.

title: Is resistance training effective to increase BDNF in multiple sclerosis? An updated systematic review and meta-analysis of isolated interventions.
abstract: Brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) is a key mediator of neuroplasticity and has been associated with disease progression in multiple sclerosis (MS). While aerobic exercise is consistently linked to BDNF modulation, the specific contribution of isolated resistance training (RT) remains unclear, as previous reviews have largely combined multimodal exercise interventions. To systematically review and meta-analyze the effects of isolated RT on peripheral BDNF levels in individuals with MS (PROSPERO: CRD420251141069). Searches were conducted in PubMed, Web of Science, Scielo, Scopus, PEDro and Cochrane up to January 10, 2026, using PICOT criteria. Controlled experimental studies investigating isolated RT and BDNF outcomes were included. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2.0 and ROBINS-I, and certainty of evidence was evaluated using GRADE. Due to methodological heterogeneity, a random-effects model was applied to estimate pooled effects. Four studies (three RCTs and one controlled non-randomized trial), totaling 126 participants with MS, were included. Interventions lasted 8-24 weeks, with training frequencies of 2-3 sessions per week. Meta-analytic synthesis revealed positive pooled effects (SMD = 0.49; 95%CI: 0.15 to 0.83; Z = 2.80; p < 0.005; I2  = 0%; Q = 1.681) with wide confidence intervals without crossing zero. With the Hartung-Knapp adjustment, due to the reduced number of studies, the analysis continued to show a positive intervention effect: (SMD = 0.49; 95%CI: 0.42 to 0.56; t = 3.716; p = 0.0339). Two studies using low-to-moderate intensity protocols (Pilates-based RT and low-load RT with bands/weights) showed significant increases in serum BDNF after 8 weeks. In contrast, studies employing higher loads (≈80% of one-repetition maximum: 1RM) demonstrated no significant BDNF changes despite functional gains. Overall certainty of evidence was rated as low due to risk of bias, inconsistency, and imprecision. Isolated RT may increase peripheral BDNF levels in individuals with MS, but this effect is supported by limited and low-certainty evidence. Furthermore, given that only four studies were included in the meta-analysis, we suggest interpreting the results with some caution.

title: CAR-T-cell therapy for autoimmune neurologic diseases.
abstract: Autoimmune neurologic diseases include multiple sclerosis, neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody-associated disease, autoimmune encephalitis, myasthenia gravis, stiff-person syndrome, chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy, and related syndromes. The contributions of B cells, plasma cells, and autoantibodies differ substantially across these disorders; however, the B-cell lineage represents a therapeutically actionable target in many of them. Chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy, originally developed for hematologic malignancies, offers a potential strategy for deep and potentially durable depletion of pathogenic B-lineage cells and subsequent immune reconstitution. In recent years, CD19, BCMA, dual-target, mRNA CAR-T-cell, and chimeric autoantibody receptor T-cell approaches have generated preliminary clinical or translational evidence, primarily in systemic autoimmune diseases. Clinical evidence in neurologic disorders remains limited and spans myasthenia gravis, NMOSD, MOGAD, multiple sclerosis, autoimmune encephalitis, stiff-person syndrome, and CIDP. This review summarizes the biologic rationale, disease-specific evidence, target selection, safety concerns, and trial-design considerations for CAR-T-cell therapy in autoimmune neurologic diseases. Current evidence supports further investigation of CAR-T cells in selected patients with highly refractory, antibody- or B-cell-driven neuroimmune disorders, but does not establish superiority over existing therapies. However, the field remains dominated by case reports and small early-phase studies, with randomized evidence currently confined to one phase 2b trial in myasthenia gravis. Establishing the risk-benefit profile will require stringent patient selection, disease-specific neurologic monitoring, controlled prospective studies, and long-term follow-up.

title: Perception of virus effects and vaccination among people with multiple sclerosis in Saudi Arabia.
abstract: BACKGROUND: People with multiple sclerosis (pwMS) are at increased risk of infection due to immune dysregulation and exposure to disease-modifying therapies (DMTs). Despite this risk, real-world vaccine uptake remains inconsistent. This study evaluated vaccination readiness, counseling practices, and infection-related perceptions among pwMS in Saudi Arabia. METHODS: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among adults with MS (n = 204) recruited using non-probability (convenience) sampling from tertiary-care clinical and community-based sources. The survey assessed demographic characteristics, vaccination attitudes and uptake, counseling experiences, perceptions of infection risk related to MS and DMTs, and awareness of Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). Internal consistency of multi-item measures was acceptable (Cronbach's α = 0.72). Descriptive statistics were used to summarize outcomes. RESULTS: The cohort was relatively young (mean age 35.7 years), with two-thirds aged 25-44 years (25-34 years: 38.2%; 35-44 years: 36.8%). Most participants held a bachelor's degree (66.7%). Attitudes toward routine vaccination were frequently non-committal: 47.6% were somewhat or very likely to vaccinate, 33.8% were neutral, and 18.6% were somewhat or very unlikely; separately, 60.8% agreed or somewhat agreed that routine vaccines might be harmful for pwMS. COVID-19 vaccination uptake was high (72.5%), whereas influenza vaccination was low (30.9%). Uptake of other adult vaccines, including hepatitis B, meningococcal, herpes zoster, and human papillomavirus vaccines, was < 10% for each. Perceived infection vulnerability was substantial, with 62.7% expressing concern about viral infections due to MS and 71.1% believing that DMTs increased susceptibility, consistent with 59.4% receiving high-efficacy DMTs. Awareness of EBV was limited: 26.5% had heard of EBV, 16.6% perceived an MS-EBV association, and 21.1% were aware of possible causality. Nearly half of participants (49.0%) were undecided about a hypothetical EBV vaccine, while approximately 44% expressed willingness to receive it. Counseling gaps were evident, as only 32.8% reported any discussion about vaccination with clinicians; counseling prior to DMT initiation and during ongoing treatment was reported by 16.2% and 19.1%, respectively. CONCLUSIONS: In a young and highly educated cohort of pwMS in Saudi Arabia, vaccine hesitancy and counseling gaps persist despite high perceived infection risk. These findings highlight the need for structured and routine vaccine counseling, particularly at MS diagnosis and before initiating high-efficacy DMTs, to improve uptake of influenza and other recommended adult vaccines in MS clinics.

title: Epstein-Barr virus shapes intrathecal Th1/Th17 immunity and parenchymal involvement in neuro-Behçet's disease.
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Human herpesviruses (HHVs) are implicated in neuro-inflammatory diseases due to their ability to establish persistent latency and reactivate in the context of immune dysregulation. Whilst Epstein -Barr virus (EBV) is recognized as a key factor in multiple sclerosis (MS), its role in neuro-Behçet's disease (NBD) remains poorly understood. METHODS: Serum and paired CSF samples were obtained from treatment-naïve patients with NBD and MS. Neurotropic viral DNA in CSF was screened by multiplex PCR. Virus-specific IgG antibodies against HSV-1 and EBV antigens (VCA and EBNA1) were measured by ELISA in serum and CSF. Real-time PCR was used to assess the expression of EBV latent genes (LMP1 and EBNA1), as well as cytokines and transcription factors, in CSF samples from NBD patients. RESULTS: In this study, we demonstrate a high prevalence of EBV DNA in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) of patients with NBD (71.43%), significantly higher than that observed in MS (35.29%), whereas other neurotropic herpesviruses are rarely detected. Notably, the presence of EBV in the CSF is not associated with a specific intrathecal humoral response, suggesting predominantly latent viral persistence and cell-mediated immune control. The concurrent expression of the latent proteins LMP1 and EBNA1 indicates a type II latency program, capable of activating interferon pathways. EBV-positive patients exhibit an immune signature characterized by significantly elevated levels of IFN-γ and IFN-α, associated with Th1/Th17 polarization and reduced FOXP3 expression, reflecting a Th17/Treg imbalance. Furthermore, EBV status is associated with distinct clinical phenotypes, with parenchymal forms being observed exclusively in EBV-positive patients. CONCLUSION: This suggests that EBV may contribute to the pathophysiology of NBD by promoting a pro-inflammatory intrathecal microenvironment. It also positions EBV as a potential biomarker and therapeutic target in this condition.

title: B-Cell-Related Neuroinflammation Across Central Nervous System Diseases: A Bibliometric and Science-Mapping Analysis, 2006-2026.
abstract: PURPOSE: Research on B cells in central nervous system (CNS) diseases rests on a mature multiple sclerosis (MS) literature, whereas evidence in CNS injury and neurodegeneration is still emerging. We mapped publications from 2006 to 2026 and separated bibliometric visibility from mechanistic maturity. METHODS: We searched the Web of Science Core Collection (WoSCC) on August 17, 2026, for English-language records carrying the Article document-type tag and published from January 1, 2006, through August 17, 2026. Two reviewers independently screened all records, with unresolved disagreements adjudicated by a third reviewer. Publication trends, collaboration, co-citation, journal flows, citation bursts, and keyword evolution were analyzed using VOSviewer, CiteSpace, bibliometrix, R, and SCImago Graphica. Search materials, parameters, and source tables were archived. RESULTS: After database-level limits, 2,701 records were screened; 467 (17.3%) were excluded and 2,234 (82.7%) included. The corpus had accrued 91,218 WoSCC citations. Annual output rose from 91 articles in 2016 to 231 in 2025; 173 articles from 2026 represent a partial year. The United States contributed the most articles, and the University of California, San Francisco ranked first after affiliation normalization. Co-citation and keyword analyses showed an MS/experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE)-centered foundation built around B-cell depletion trials, meningeal pathology, diagnostic criteria, and regulatory B-cell biology. Recent bursts included anti-CD20 therapy, single-cell RNA sequencing, autoimmune encephalitis, ischemic stroke, Mendelian randomization, B-cell depletion, and Alzheimer disease. CONCLUSION: B-cell-related CNS research has expanded, but evidence maturity remains disease-specific. MS/EAE provides the clearest foundation. Findings in CNS injury, neurodegeneration, and candidate peripheral-CNS routes remain context-dependent and require validation by disease, anatomical compartment, B-cell state, and stage. Bibliometric prominence reveals attention, not shared causality or therapeutic efficacy.

title: Multiple sclerosis relapse following gamma knife radiosurgery for meningioma in a patient treated with natalizumab: case report.
abstract: OBJECTIVES: We describe a case of a patient with multiple sclerosis (MS) stable on natalizumab who developed widespread gadolinium-enhancing lesions and clinical relapse seven and eight months after gamma knife radiosurgery (GKRS) for left cerebellar convexity meningioma. We explore how increased blood-brain barrier (BBB) permeability post-GKRS could potentially interfere with the lymphocyte anti-trafficking effect of natalizumab and result in new central nervous system (CNS) inflammation distant from the radiation site. METHODS: Comprehensive analysis of the patient's chart, brain and spine imaging, serum and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) profiles was conducted. We compiled a graphical representation of treatment changes, radiologic findings, and GKRS initiation within one timeframe. We conducted a structured literature review to support the discussion of this case and hypothesize possible pathophysiological mechanisms contributing to clinical and radiological findings. RESULTS: Seven months after GKRS, follow-up brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated multiple gadolinium-enhancing lesions in both cerebral hemispheres, and repeat imaging one month later revealed new gadolinium-enhancing lesions, correlating with the patient's clinical relapse. Alternative causes of disease progression, including radiation-induced demyelination, radionecrosis, opportunistic infections, progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML), and development of anti-natalizumab antibodies, were explored and considered less likely. The patient was switched to ofatumumab with subsequent clinical and radiological stability. DISCUSSION: Given extensive new inflammatory lesions far from the GKRS site, it seems unlikely that the sole mechanism was radiation-induced neurotoxicity. We hypothesize that late delayed radiation side effects caused by GKRS may have enabled peripheral lymphocytes to enter the CNS, counteracting the effects of natalizumab on blocking lymphocyte trafficking through the BBB and possibly contributing to MS relapse.

title: Cellular senescence in multiple sclerosis: hallmarks, immunosenescence, and therapeutic implications.
abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an immune-mediated neurodegenerative disease where chronological aging predicts the conversion to progressive MS (PMS), a phase defined by compartmentalized inflammation and accelerated neurodegeneration. While current disease modifying therapies (DMTs) are effective for managing the inflammatory aspect of MS, treatments remain inadequate. It is imperative to understand the biology of aging including an important hallmark of aging, cellular senescence. Cellular senescence is a state of cell cycle arrest where cells remain in their senescent state and produce a distinctive senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), characterized by the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, chemokines, and growth factors. Growing experimental and clinical evidence suggests that the accumulation of senescent cells and SASP secretion perpetuates a pathological feedback loop linking age-related processes with accelerated neurodegeneration observed in PMS. Whether senescence drives PMS or accompanies it remains unresolved. In this Review, we outline the biology of aging, senescence pathway markers, and SASP components. We evaluate studies of cellular senescence and SASP markers in MS, including immunosenescence, T- and B-cell changes; the contributions of Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, and herpes simplex virus-1; and the relationship between senescence burden, brain atrophy, and DMT response. Lastly, we outline the available senotherapeutic approaches aimed at mitigating MS and other neurodegenerative diseases.

title: Targeting TLR4 alleviates the progression of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis by regulating central resident cells and Th1/Th17 cell differentiation.
abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an autoimmune demyelinating disease characterized by neuroinflammation. Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) is a receptor for damage-associated molecular patterns, such as high-mobility group box 1 (HMGB1) and plays a role in innate immunity. However, its precise role and cellular dynamics in MS pathogenesis are unclear. Using the experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) model, we mapped the expression dynamics of TLR4 and found that in the spinal cords, the cell type associated with the disease shifted from neurons to activated glia. To establish causality, we subjected

title: Thalamic atrophy in active and inactive secondary progressive multiple sclerosis patients: A comparative study.
abstract: Thalamic atrophy may be an indicator of neurodegeneration in people with secondary progressive multiple sclerosis (pwSPMS). The atrophy usually begins asymmetrically, and the thalamic asymmetry index (TAI) can be used to estimate the severity of neurodegeneration. SPMS is commonly divided into two groups of active and inactive. No study has compared TAI between SPMS groups and examine its relationships with cognitive and motor measures in pwSPMS. This study aimed to compare the TAI between active and inactive pwSPMS and to examine its relationship with key clinical, cognitive, and motor variables. In this cross-sectional study, 38 pwSPMS (15 active and 23 inactive) were enrolled from February to November 2024. MRI-based volumetric measurements were used to determine thalamic volumes and calculate the TAI. Cognitive and motor tests, including the SDMT, PASAT, and 9HPT were also administered alongside clinical examinations. Active SPMS patients had significantly lower NTV compared to inactive patients (Cohen's d = -1.58, p < 0.001). No significant difference in TAI was observed between groups. NTV correlated with cognitive scores in both active (r = 0.74, P = 0.002) and inactive (r = 0.65, p < 0.001) groups and with disability in the inactive group (r = -0.5, P= 0.014). Active SPMS patients showed worse cognitive and motor performance. Thalamic atrophy is more severe in active SPMS and is associated with worse cognitive and motor outcomes. While thalamic asymmetry did not differentiate between subgroups, it may serve as a marker for functional status in SPMS.

title: Review Article: A Scientific Journey with Zelig Eshhar at the Dawn of Monoclonal Antibody Research.
abstract: Professor Zelig Eshhar, a colleague, collaborator, and dear friend, is known worldwide as the visionary who laid the foundations for chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy, a breakthrough that transformed cancer immunotherapy. Long before this revolutionary achievement, however, Zelig profoundly influenced research at the Weizmann Institute of Science by introducing the then state-of-the-art hybridoma technology for the generation of monoclonal antibodies (mAbs), which he brought directly from the oven of Nobel laureates Georges KÃ¶hler and CÃ©sar Milstein. Through his expertise and the dedication of his legendary team, Tova Waks, his indispensable partner for 55 years, Orith Gigi-Leitner, and Sara Barak, this technology rapidly became an invaluable resource for investigators throughout the Institute. My collaboration with Zelig during the 1980s led to the generation of monoclonal antibodies against a series of biologically important proteins, including interferons, other cytokines, their soluble receptors, the unique IL-18 Binding Protein (IL-18BP), and, years later, glutamate oxaloacetate transaminase 1 (GOT1). These antibodies proved to be remarkably versatile research tools, suitable for neutralization, affinity chromatography, immunoassays, flow cytometry, immunoblotting, and numerous other applications. Most importantly, they enabled the affinity purification of in-house corresponding recombinant cytokines. The antibodies proved far more than analytical reagents. They became indispensable tools for both basic research and translational medicine. Together, these unique reagents formed the foundation of a ligand-affinity strategy that led to the discovery of previously unknown cytokine receptors and binding proteins. Those include the type I interferon receptor, the second TNF receptor (TBPII), and the unexpected IL-18 Binding Protein. These discoveries not only advanced our understanding of cytokine biology but also paved the way for therapeutics such as RebifŴ, EnbrelŴ, RemicadeŴ and Tadekinig alfaTM, used in the treatment of autoimmune, inflammatory, and genetic diseases, such as multiple sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis and Crohn's disease. While our scientific paths diverged in 1989, Zelig's toward the revolutionary concept of chimeric antigen receptors and mine toward cytokine receptors and binding proteins, they ultimately converged again as TNF and IL-18BP antagonists found applications in enhancement of CAR-T therapy and in management of potential inflammatory complications associated with this therapy. This chapter stands as a testament to Zelig's vision in introducing and advancing monoclonal antibody technology at the Weizmann Institute.

title: Photobiomodulation as a regulator of neuroinflammation: mechanistic insights and therapeutic potential in brain disorders.
abstract: Brain disorders, including neurodegenerative, neuropsychiatric, and cerebrovascular diseases, represent a growing global health challenge contributing to disability and mortality worldwide. Although these conditions differ in etiology and clinical presentation, accumulating evidence identifies neuroinflammation as a shared pathological mechanism. Involving microglial activation, astrocytic reactivity, cytokine dysregulation, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and blood-brain barrier disruption, it contributes to synaptic dysfunction, neuronal loss, and disease progression, yet therapeutic strategies targeting these processes remain limited. Photobiomodulation (PBM), the therapeutic application of low-intensity red to near-infrared light, has emerged as a neurotechnology capable of modulating biological pathways relevant to neuroinflammation. Preclinical studies suggest that PBM may influence mitochondrial activity through cytochrome c oxidase-mediated mechanisms, enhancing cellular metabolism while regulating reactive oxygen species, inflammatory signaling pathways, and tissue homeostasis. Through these effects, PBM may attenuate neuroinflammatory responses, regulate glial activation, and support neuroprotective processes across multiple neurological models. This narrative review examines evidence supporting neuroinflammation as a common denominator across major brain disorders and explores the biological rationale for PBM as a therapeutic strategy. It summarizes the cellular and molecular basis of PBM, its effects on neuroinflammatory pathways, and preclinical and clinical findings across brain disease models. Preclinical findings consistently support a multi-target anti-inflammatory effect, whereas clinical investigation remains at an early stage, with encouraging results in Alzheimer's disease and multiple sclerosis but mainly negative data on primary outcomes in Parkinson's disease and major depressive disorder. Further research is needed to optimize treatment parameters, clarify mechanisms of action, and determine clinical efficacy across disease contexts.

title: A Case of Treatment-Refractory Tumefactive Multiple Sclerosis Mimicking Brain Abscess.
abstract: A 47-year-old female presented with one week of left facial numbness following recent dental extractions. Initial brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with and without contrast revealed a contrast-enhancing lesion in the right parieto-occipital lobe with mild diffusion restriction and surrounding vasogenic edema, as well as smaller enhancing lesions in the right frontal and parietal lobes. Empiric intravenous (IV) antibiotic treatment was started due to a high concern for odontogenic brain abscesses. Despite antibiotic treatment, repeat brain MRI revealed new contrast-enhancing lesions in the left pons and cerebellar peduncle, suggesting that infection was unlikely and antibiotics were discontinued. The differential diagnosis broadened to neoplastic, inflammatory, and demyelinating pathologies. A brain biopsy of the right occipital lobe lesion was pursued for a definitive diagnosis. Following the brain biopsy, the patient received five days of IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily, followed by a two-week oral prednisone taper with clinical improvement. Brain biopsy subsequently demonstrated macrophages, reactive lymphocytosis, and astrogliosis with loss of myelin, confirming the diagnosis of tumefactive multiple sclerosis (TMS). Over the subsequent two years, she experienced recurrent flares of TMS with new demyelinating lesions despite disease-modifying therapy (DMT) with ocrelizumab, resulting in progressive disability accrual. Upon transition to natalizumab, disease remission was achieved. This case highlights the diagnostic challenges of TMS as it may radiographically resemble odontogenic brain abscesses, particularly in the setting of recent dental infections. Brain biopsy may be required when neuroimaging and cerebrospinal fluid findings are inconclusive. This case also suggests that natalizumab may be considered in selected treatment-refractory cases, although further evidence is needed.

title: Agreement and longitudinal repeatability of established brain volumetry pipelines across healthy controls, multiple sclerosis, and Alzheimer's disease.
abstract: Brain volume estimates are increasingly used as longitudinal endpoints in neuroimaging studies and clinical trials, but outputs from different segmentation pipelines may not be interchangeable. In this study, we performed a version-specific comparison of six established brain segmentation pipelines across healthy controls (HC; FreeSurfer v6, FreeSurfer v7.2, SAMSEG, FastSurfer v1, SIENAX/SIENA-XL, and CAT12 were evaluated. The primary aims were to quantify systematic offsets and inter-pipeline agreement in normalized baseline volume estimates, assess within-pipeline repeatability and longitudinal change-from-baseline concordance, and determine whether longitudinal processing reduced variability relative to cross-sectional processing. Gray matter, white matter, hippocampus, and thalamus were selected and normalized to intracranial volume. Agreement was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients, while longitudinal change was evaluated using mixed-effects models and repeatability metrics. Baseline volume estimates differed significantly across pipelines in 11 of 12 cohort-by-tissue comparisons (FDR-adjusted Together, these findings show that systematic offset, absolute agreement, longitudinal change magnitude, and short-interval repeatability represent distinct properties of volumetric pipelines and vary by tissue, cohort, and processing mode. Longitudinal processing reduced variability but not uniformly, highlighting pipeline- and tissue-dependent differences relevant to the interpretation of longitudinal volumetric measurements.

title: The "Invisible Killer" of Neurodegeneration: Mitochondrial Dysfunction in Neurodegenerative Disorders, Mechanisms, Emerging Pathways and Therapeutic Strategies.
abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson's disease (PD), Alzheimer's disease (AD), Huntington's disease (HD), multiple sclerosis (MS), and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) place substantial burden on global public health. Mounting evidence identifies mitochondrial dysfunction as a central contributor to neuronal damage and progressive brain functional decline. As a narrative review, this work aims to dissect mitochondrial‑associated pathological features across these major neurodegenerative disorders, summarize under‑recognized emerging mechanisms, and highlight translational bottlenecks for mitochondrial‑targeted therapies. Mitochondria sustain neuronal survival by mediating oxidative‑phosphorylation‑driven energy production, biomolecule biosynthesis, calcium homeostasis, reactive oxygen species (ROS) metabolism, and apoptotic regulation. In PD, aggregated α‑synuclein (α‑syn) damages respiratory‑chain complex I, perturbs mitochondrial dynamics and blocks PINK1/Parkin‑dependent mitophagy. In AD, amyloid‑β together with hyper‑phosphorylated tau (p-Tau) impairs respiratory complex activity, axonal mitochondrial trafficking and mitophagic clearance. Mutant huntingtin induces multiple mitochondrial lesions in HD, while inflammation‑triggered oxidative stress secondarily compromises mitochondrial function in MS. Pathogenic mutations in ALS disrupt respiratory‑chain assembly, mitochondrial dynamics and mitophagy. Beyond classic mitochondrial defects including respiratory‑chain impairment, dynamic imbalance and defective mitophagy, emerging mechanisms such as mitocytosis, mitochondrial aminoacyl‑tRNA synthetase (mt‑aaRS) dysfunction and mitochondria‑associated membrane (MAM) disruption are discussed. Mitochondrial dysfunction drives neurodegeneration via energy exhaustion, aggravated oxidative stress, pathological protein aggregation and excessive neuronal apoptosis. We further recapitulate mitochondrial‑oriented therapeutic approaches including small‑molecule regulators, mitophagy activators, mitochondrial biogenesis promoters, gene‑editing strategies and mitochondrial transplantation. Notable translational obstacles remain, including limited blood‑brain‑barrier penetration of candidate drugs, narrow therapeutic time‑window post‑symptom onset, and prominent disease heterogeneity. By synthesizing basic experimental findings and pre‑clinical and clinical trial progress, this review provides updated insights into the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative diseases and facilitates the development of precise mitochondrial‑targeted therapeutic regimens.

title: Computational identification of EBNA1-binding candidates using machine learning-based virtual screening and molecular docking.
abstract: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is associated with several malignancies and multiple sclerosis, and Epstein-Barr nuclear antigen 1 (EBNA1) plays an essential role in viral genome replication and episome maintenance. The experimentally characterized KVD-associated pocket within the EBNA1 DNA-binding domain provides a structurally defined site for computational ligand prioritization. This study aimed to identify and prioritize predicted EBNA1-binding candidates using an integrated machine-learning and structure-based virtual screening framework. A PubChem EBNA1 bioactivity dataset comprising 304,124 records was curated to obtain 4,584 unique compounds. Molecular representation combined 1,024-bit Morgan fingerprints with 11 RDKit molecular descriptors. Random Forest, SVM-RBF, Logistic Regression, and XGBoost models were evaluated using scaffold-based independent testing. The optimized XGBoost model was applied to a non-overlapping DrugBank library of 12,287 compounds. Compounds with predicted activity probabilities ≥0.5 were subjected to Lipinski-based filtering, followed by molecular docking against the KVD-associated binding pocket of EBNA1 (PDB ID: 6NPM). Docking validation was performed by independent KVD redocking at exhaustiveness values of 8, 16, and 32. Post-docking candidates were further evaluated using PAINS, aggregation, frequent-hitter/promiscuity, assay-interference, redox-associated structural-alert, and ADMET assessments. XGBoost demonstrated the highest test-set ROC-AUC (0.835), PR-AUC (0.408), and best Brier score (0.067), and was selected for virtual screening. Screening identified 116 compounds above the probability threshold, of which 40 satisfied Lipinski criteria and were docked. Thirty-two compounds achieved docking scores ≤ -7.0 kcal/mol. Sequential liability assessment and integrated prioritization identified 10 computationally prioritized EBNA1-binding candidates with favorable combined machine-learning, docking, and structural-filter profiles. The integrated computational framework enabled systematic prioritization of structurally diverse predicted EBNA1-binding candidates for further experimental investigation. The identified candidates represent computationally prioritized molecules for subsequent biochemical and functional evaluation of EBNA1 binding and activity and should not be interpreted as experimentally validated antiviral or disease-modifying agents. Virtual screening for drug discovery using trained ML model for EBNA1 protein, Molecular Docking, and ADMET analysis.

title: Revisiting the MS paradox: automated 2.5D FLAIR segmentation and DTI microstructural profiling reveals dissociation between lesion burden and reference-like intralesional tract profiles.
abstract: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) reveals macroscopic lesion burden in multiple sclerosis (MS) but correlates poorly with clinical phenotype, a phenomenon known as the clinico-radiological paradox. While diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) metrics assess microstructural damage, standard whole-lesion averaging may obscure microstructurally spared white matter within heterogeneous plaques. We propose a fully automated, multimodal pipeline to identify and quantify reference-like intralesional segments (RLIS) within MS lesions (i.e., the cluster exhibiting maximum feature-space similarity to subject-specific, lesion-spared reference tissue). A modified 2.5D U-Net, developed and evaluated on a cohort of 75 MS patients (115 series), performed automated FLAIR lesion segmentation. In an independent cohort of 100 MS subjects, intralesional DTI metrics (FA and MD) were extracted along streamlines reconstructed via Constrained Spherical Deconvolution tractography. Unsupervised clustering algorithms, validated against a subject-specific, lesion-spared reference CST streamlines (internal capsule), identified operationally defined reference-like segments. The 2.5D U-Net achieved robust segmentation performance (DSC: 0.732, VC: 0.954), exhibited higher nominal metrics in a contextual benchmark comparison (DSC: 0.682, VC: 0.864). Across the clinical cohort, lesion count (11-131) and volume (0.54-57.3 mL) varied widely. Among the evaluated clustering methods, K-Means and Gaussian Mixture Models proved to be the most conservative, identifying median reference-like segment proportions of 26% and 22%, respectively. Crucially, the proportion of reference-like intralesional segments showed no significant monotonic association with macroscopic lesion volume or count. This automated framework successfully integrates robust deep learning-based lesion segmentation with tract-specific analysis to quantify the proportion of reference-like intralesional segments. The observed dissociation between overall lesion burden and RLIS suggests that this index serves as a promising candidate metric for exploring microstructural features that may contribute to the clinico-radiological paradox.

title: Association between psychosocial consequences of visual dysfunction and depressive symptom burden in multiple sclerosis and neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder.
abstract: Visual dysfunction and depressive symptoms are common and often disabling manifestations of multiple sclerosis (MS) and neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD). In this multicenter cross-sectional study, 458 adults with MS (

title: Changes in vaccination status, willingness and knowledge in patients with multiple sclerosis: Results from a five-year longitudinal study.
abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic immune-mediated disease requiring long-term management. Both the disease itself and disease-modifying therapies increase susceptibility to severe infections. Ensuring adequate vaccination in patients with MS is therefore essential. However, vaccine hesitancy and suboptimal vaccination coverage remain major clinical challenges. To comprehensively evaluate changes in vaccination status, vaccination willingness and vaccination-related knowledge in patients with MS over a five-year interval spanning the pre-/early and post-pandemic periods of coronavirus disease 2019, and to identify factors associated with vaccination status and vaccine uptake. Longitudinal observational cohort study at a single German MS center. Patients with MS ( The patient cohort was predominantly female (70.3%) and had a mean age of 45.8 years and a median disease duration of 7 years at baseline. General vaccination willingness declined from 81.1% at baseline to 66.3% at follow-up ( Despite intensified vaccination counseling, vaccination willingness declined markedly, suggesting post-pandemic vaccination fatigue in patients with MS. Persistent discrepancies between perceived and documented vaccination status and the impact of vaccine-related concerns highlight the need for more targeted strategies to strengthen vaccination confidence and improve immunization coverage.

title: Utility of extracellular vesicles in the diagnosis of central nervous system diseases.
abstract: Central nervous system (CNS) disorders encompass a diverse spectrum of conditions characterized by intricate pathological mechanisms, and the presence of the blood-brain barrier (BBB) has long impeded early diagnosis. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are lipid bilayer nanoparticles released by living cells that can encapsulate and transport bioactive molecules such as proteins and nucleic acids across the BBB. EVs can be detected in biofluids such as blood and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) through non-invasive or minimally invasive assays, and have emerged as highly promising vehicles for CNS liquid biopsies. Recent studies demonstrate that specific EV-associated protein cargoes (e.g., phosphorylated tau, α-syn) and non-coding RNAs (e.g., miR-422a, miR-409-3p) exhibit distinct differential expression profiles across various pathologies. These molecular signatures hold promise for early detection, differential diagnosis, and disease staging, with some biomarker panels showing high diagnostic accuracy. However, whether they outperform conventional CSF biomarkers still requires direct comparison and validation within the same cohorts. This review highlights recent research advances in the use of EVs for the diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease, briefly touches upon other CNS disorders including stroke, glioma, multiple sclerosis, Huntington's disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and discusses the clinical translational potential and remaining challenges of EV-based diagnostics.

title: Case Report: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis presenting as a multiple sclerosis mimic.
abstract: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA) rarely involves the central nervous system and may closely resemble inflammatory demyelinating disease. We report a 32-year-old woman with adult-onset asthma and recurrent sinusitis who presented with bilateral lower-extremity sensory symptoms and neuropathic pain. Brain and spinal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated multifocal T2-hyperintense lesions fulfilling dissemination in space and time according to the 2017 McDonald criteria. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis revealed mild pleocytosis, CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands, and eosinophils on qualitative cytological examination. Multiple sclerosis (MS) was initially suspected and intravenous methylprednisolone resulted in partial improvement. Three weeks later, the patient developed palpable purpura, inflammatory arthralgia, and left foot-elevating paresis. Follow-up MRI demonstrated a new enhancing lesion and electrophysiological studies revealed axonal neuropathy. Retrospective review of the initial laboratory results showed that peripheral eosinophilia was already present at baseline, while subsequent evaluation identified eosinophilic gastritis on gastroscopic biopsy and eosinophilic bone marrow infiltration. The diagnosis of EGPA was established based on the clinical presentation, laboratory findings, and histopathological evidence of eosinophilic inflammation, and the patient fulfilled the 2022 ACR/EULAR classification criteria for EGPA. Treatment with corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide followed by maintenance mepolizumab resulted in sustained clinical stability. This case highlights that EGPA may present with radiological and CSF-findings suggestive of MS and emphasizes the importance of integrating systemic manifestations to avoid diagnostic delay.

title: AQP4 antibody-induced astrocyte injury reshapes CNS immune architecture in a combined EAE-AQP4-IgG model of neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder.
abstract: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) and multiple sclerosis (MS) are inflammatory autoimmune diseases of the central nervous system (CNS) that share demyelinating features but differ fundamentally in pathogenesis. The discovery of neuromyelitis optica immunoglobulin G antibodies (NMO-IgG) that target aquaporin-4 (AQP4) established NMOSD as a distinct clinical entity, although the experimental platforms used to dissect the mechanistic basis of this disorder remain insufficiently defined. Thus, this study aimed to develop a combined EAE-AQP4-IgG model by intrathecally delivering patient-derived NMO-IgG and human complement into pre-immunized mice to compare the associated pathology with that of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE), a representative model of MS. Both models exhibited blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption, reflected by altered ZO-1 and CD31 expression. Notably, glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) was strongly upregulated in EAE, whereas in the combined EAE-AQP4-IgG model, GFAP was acutely lost, indicating antibody-mediated astrocyte destruction. Consistently, AQP4 expression was markedly reduced in combined EAE-AQP4-IgG model animals. Combined EAE-AQP4-IgG model mice also displayed more severe demyelination and inflammation, confirmed by Luxol Fast Blue and H&E staining, electron microscopy, and MBP/Iba1 immunostaining. Quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) further revealed distinct inflammatory signatures:

title: Effects of knee muscle fatigue on gait and proprioception in multiple sclerosis.
abstract: People with multiple sclerosis often experience muscle weakness and fatigue, which impair proprioception and gait. The effects of knee muscle fatigue on these outcomes remain unclear. This study investigated the effects of a knee muscle fatigue protocol on knee position sense and gait in people with multiple sclerosis. A total of 36 mildly affected people with multiple sclerosis and nine healthy controls participated in this case-control study with repeated pre- and post-fatigue assessments. Gait was assessed using a G-Walk sensor, and knee position sense with an active repositioning test on an isokinetic dynamometer. Muscle strength and fatigue indexes were determined isokinetically for the knee flexors and extensors. During the fatigue protocol, people with multiple sclerosis produced lower total workloads than healthy control, although fatigue indexes were similar. After fatigue, both groups showed increased cadence and reduced gait cycle duration, while gait speed increased only in people with multiple sclerosis. Knee position sense deteriorated bilaterally in people with multiple sclerosis and on the non-dominant side in healthy control. Localized knee muscle fatigue altered knee position sense and gait in both groups, with no significant group×time interaction, though the small control group warrants caution. Similar fatigue indices despite lower total work warrant cautious interpretation of the Cybex fatigue index, given its dependence on baseline torque. As proprioceptive acuity declined transiently after localized knee muscle fatigue, clinicians may consider performing balance- or coordination-demanding tasks beforehand in people with multiple sclerosis.

title: Automated optic chiasm segmentation in magnetic resonance imaging of multiple sclerosis patients using a multi-view, multi-class U-Net with limited annotated data.
journal: Journal of research in medical sciences : the official journal of Isfahan University of Medical Sciences
abstract: Accurate magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-based segmentation of the optic chiasm is essential for the quantitative assessment of visual pathway damage in multiple sclerosis (MS). However, accurate segmentation remains challenging because of the structure's small size, complex anatomy, and marked foreground-background imbalance. Existing deep learning approaches often rely on single-view imaging and may not fully exploit complementary anatomical information across MRI planes. To address these limitations, we developed and evaluated a novel multi-view two-dimensional U-Net (2D U-Net) framework that jointly leverages axial and coronal MRI information within a unified segmentation architecture for automated optic chiasm segmentation. In this secondary analysis, a novel multi-view 2D U-Net framework was developed for optic chiasm segmentation by integrating axial and coronal MRI images within a unified three-class segmentation architecture. Models were optimized using a Tversky loss function and evaluated using five-fold patient-wise cross-validation. Segmentation performance was assessed quantitatively using multiple metrics, with the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC), intersection over union (IoU), and balanced accuracy serving as the primary evaluation metrics, and qualitatively through visual comparison with expert annotations. A total of 58 patients with relapsing-remitting MS were included in the analysis. The proposed multi-view model demonstrated stable convergence and achieved the highest segmentation performance among all evaluated models, with a DSC of 91.28%, IoU of 84.05%, and balanced accuracy of 94.43%. Compared with the best-performing single-view model, the multi-view approach improved DSC and IoU by approximately 13 and 19 percentage points, respectively. Qualitative assessment showed closer agreement between multi-view segmentations and expert annotations. The proposed multi-view, multi-class 2D U-Net framework outperformed conventional single-view models for optic chiasm segmentation. These findings demonstrate that integrating complementary anatomical information from axial and coronal MRI planes can substantially improve segmentation performance. The results indicate the potential of multi-view learning for the automated segmentation of small and anatomically complex structures.

title: A two year clinical, immunological and gut-brain-axis prospective study to predict treatment response to cladribine tablets in relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis.
abstract: In relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS) it is challenging to predict which person will benefit from a certain therapy, such as cladribine tablets (CladT). This study aimed to obtain a better understanding of the interaction between the gut-brain axis and CladT to improve treatment response prediction. In this multicenter, prospective, observational study, we included 81 people with RRMS starting CladT. We assessed the clinical, immunological and microbiological profiles at baseline and after 3, 12 and 24 months, and compared results between responders and non-responders, classified based on inflammatory disease activity and disability progression (NEDA-3). A total of 35 of 81 (47%) participants were responders. We found no differences in immune cell profiles between responders and non-responders. Network analysis revealed more positive correlations between immune cell clusters within the same parent cluster and a stronger negative correlation between CD8 Although we found a trend toward more coordinated immune reorganization in CladT responders, and identified fecal alpha diversity and fecal

title: Targeting P2Y(12) limits T(H)17 accumulation in the CNS and reduces EAE progression.
abstract: Platelets are increasingly recognized as active amplifiers of neuroinflammation in multiple sclerosis and experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE). P2Y12 is an essential ADP receptor that regulates platelet activation and is upregulated in neuroinflammatory lesions. However, its contribution across different effector populations and therapeutic potential in autoimmune diseases of the central nervous system (CNS) remain incompletely defined. Therefore, we characterized P2ry12 expression across different immune and CNS-resident effector populations involved in EAE. To define P2Y12-dependent mechanisms in autoimmune neuroinflammation, we targeted the P2Y12 receptor both genetically and pharmacologically in MOG35-55-induced EAE and monitored disease course and immunopathology. The neuroinflammatory response was profiled by flow cytometry, histology, and cytokine analyses. Pharmacological inhibition with elinogrel or clopidogrel was evaluated in prophylactic and therapeutic treatment regimens. Additionally, prophylactic elinogrel treatment was combined with antibody-mediated platelet depletion during the effector phase of EAE to define the contribution of platelets to the observed effects. Among the immune and CNS-resident effector populations examined, platelets exhibited the highest abundance of P2ry12 transcripts, and platelet P2ry12 expression increased following EAE induction. Consistent with a proinflammatory role of the P2Y12 receptor in CNS autoimmunity, its genetic deficiency was associated with decreased disease progression, as indicated by lower peak and cumulative scores, while disease onset remained unchanged compared to wild-type mice. Pharmacological inhibition of the P2Y12 receptor reproduced this protective effect. Importantly, treatment with elinogrel did not affect the number of infiltrated platelets, but markedly reduced cellular infiltration and demyelination. Furthermore, the protective effect was associated with a significant reduction in infiltrating CD4+ T cells, particularly pro-inflammatory T helper 17 (TH17) cells. Of note, elinogrel provided no additional benefit beyond platelet depletion, a finding compatible with a platelet-mediated contribution to the observed effect. Clopidogrel, another P2Y12 inhibitor, similarly reduced disease severity when administered prophylactically. Of note, both elinogrel and clopidogrel remained effective when treatment was initiated after clinical onset. These data identify platelet-associated P2Y12 signaling as a functionally relevant amplifier of EAE pathology. P2Y12 blockade limits CNS immune infiltration and neuroinflammation-induced tissue injury, exerts an impact on the TH17 axis, and retains efficacy when administered therapeutically. Collectively, these findings support P2Y12 as a mechanistically grounded and translationally relevant target in CNS autoimmunity.

title: Clinical characteristics, disability outcomes, and disease-modifying therapy patterns in late-onset multiple sclerosis: a single-center retrospective cohort study.
abstract: Late-onset multiple sclerosis (LOMS), defined here as symptom onset at age 50 years or later, is associated with diagnostic complexity, a higher prevalence of progressive phenotypes, greater disability, and challenging disease-modifying therapy (DMT) decisions. We characterized clinical manifestations, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) lesion distribution, disability outcomes, and DMT patterns in a Latvian tertiary-care cohort. We retrospectively reviewed medical records from Riga East University Hospital. Of 518 patients in the source multiple sclerosis dataset, 59 met the LOMS definition; after exclusion of two patients with clinically isolated syndrome and one with an unspecified phenotype, 56 patients with relapsing-remitting, primary progressive, or secondary progressive multiple sclerosis were analyzed. Clinical symptoms, MRI lesion localization, baseline and five-year Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) scores, EDSS change, and initial and current DMT patterns were assessed using nonparametric and exact tests. The cohort included 38 women and 18 men; 38 patients had relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis and 18 had progressive multiple sclerosis. Progressive phenotypes were associated with more frequent pyramidal/motor symptoms (100.0% vs. 76.3%; Progressive LOMS phenotypes were associated with greater motor and sphincter symptom burden and higher disability, but the absence of a difference in unadjusted EDSS change should not be interpreted as equivalent disability progression. Treatment associations primarily describe real-world selection and are subject to confounding by indication.

title: [Effect of cyclic phosphatidic acid on hypoxia and its potential medical applications].
journal: Nihon yakurigaku zasshi. Folia pharmacologica Japonica
abstract: Cyclic phosphatidic acid (cPA) is a bioactive lipid containing a cyclic phosphate group at the sn-2,3 position of the glycerol backbone. cPA exhibits neurotrophic factor-like activity in hippocampal neurons in vitro, and we have been developing therapeutic agents that exploits its neuroprotective properties. Among the synthesized cPA derivatives, 2-carba-cPA (2ccPA) emerged as a promising candidate, and its functions in the brain has been investigated in various animal models. Cerebrovascular disease involves impaired cerebral blood flow that reduces oxygen supply and leads to neuronal dysfunction. We hypothesized that the neuroprotective actions of 2ccPA would extend to delayed neuronal death following transient cerebral ischemia. In a rat model of transient ischemia, 2ccPA significantly suppressed delayed neuronal death and glial activation. Further studies showed that 2ccPA suppresses hypoxia-induced neuronal cell death in vitro. In other animal models, 2ccPA reduced demyelination and glial activation in multiple sclerosis, and mitigated neuroinflammation in traumatic brain injury and neuropsychiatric systemic lupus erythematosus. These findings indicate that 2ccPA exerts broad neuroprotective effects across diverse brain pathologies. Pharmacokinetic analysis revealed that 2ccPA reaches the brain within 20 minutes after intraperitoneal administration and is subsequently degraded to 2-carba-lysophosphatidic acid (2cLPA), suggesting that both 2ccPA and 2cLPA may contribute to the physiological activity of 2ccPA in vivo. Ongoing studies aim to further define the functions of 2cLPA. In this paper, we introduce the protective effect of 2ccPA on transient ischemia. And we also present the latest findings regarding its efficacy in frontotemporal dementia, and potential clinical application of 2ccPA.

title: Case Report: Feasibility of clinic-to-home multichannel FES-assisted gait rehabilitation in secondary progressive multiple sclerosis.
abstract: Functional electrical stimulation (FES) is used as an adjunct to gait rehabilitation in people with multiple sclerosis (PwMS), but most approaches target a single muscle group. This case report describes the feasibility, tolerability, and observed functional changes associated with a novel multichannel FES (NeuroSkin®) system, to our knowledge the first report of its use across clinic-to-home phases in PwMS, in a 61-year-old woman with secondary progressive multiple sclerosis (EDSS 6) with gait and balance impairment requiring a cane for community ambulation. This retrospective case report analyzed prospectively collected routine-care data covering an 18-week multimodal FES-assisted rehabilitation program comprising 58 sessions of 60-80 min each: a 7-week clinic-based phase (23 sessions), a 6-week supervised home-based phase (20 sessions), and a 5-week unsupervised home-based phase (15 sessions). Sessions included motor imagery, sit-to-stand training, FES-assisted cycling, and overground gait training. Multichannel stimulation was delivered in a gait-phase-specific manner (40 Hz; pulse widths 200-400 µs) according to muscle group. Functional outcomes were assessed at baseline (PRE), after the clinic-based (MID1), supervised home-based (MID2), and unsupervised home-based (POST) phases, using the Functional Reach Test (FRT), 10-m Walk Test, and Timed Up and Go (TUG); data were analyzed descriptively. No serious adverse events occurred; the participant experienced transient skin redness, and device deficiencies in 3 of 58 sessions, all resolved without affecting completion. Walking speed on the 10-m Walk Test increased from 0.53 to 1.04 m·s⁻ Despite inherent limitations of a single retrospective case report, these findings indicate that a multichannel FES-assisted rehabilitation program is feasible and well tolerated in a person with advanced SPMS across care settings; controlled studies are needed to establish efficacy.

title: Case Report: Blurring the immunological border in the diagnostic evaluation of optic neuritis.
abstract: Optic neuritis (ON) is a common inflammatory syndrome that may represent the initial manifestation of multiple sclerosis (MS), myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody-associated disease (MOGAD), or other autoimmune disorders. Although serological testing and imaging criteria have improved diagnostic accuracy, early immunological and radiological findings may overlap, creating diagnostic uncertainty with relevant therapeutic implications. A 48-year-old woman presented with sudden, painless monocular visual loss. Orbital MRI showed optic perineuritis with perineural dural enhancement. The combination of optic perineuritis and subsequent optic nerve involvement initially suggested a MOGAD-like phenotype or Ischemic Optic Neuropathy. Although extensive immunological screening found a strong positivity of anti-β This case illustrates how early immunological and radiological red flags may suggest other systemic autoimmune diseases despite eventual confirmation of MS. The diagnostic pathway was shaped by the temporal evolution of imaging and biomarker findings rather than by isolated baseline features. The observation emphasizes the risk of premature diagnostic labelling in seronegative optic neuritis and highlights the need for cautious interpretation of early red flags within a longitudinal framework. At the immunological border in the diagnostic evaluation of optic neuritis, early phenotypic presentations may not reliably predict final disease classification. Longitudinal integration of clinical evolution, imaging findings, and biomarker data is essential to achieve diagnostic certainty and guide appropriate long-term treatment decisions. This case supports a dynamic, evidence-based diagnostic approach in atypical immune-mediated optic neuritis.

title: Is it time for anti-CD20 discontinuation in multiple sclerosis? Cumulative risk or cumulative uncertainty.
abstract: The widespread adoption of anti-CD20 monoclonal antibodies (anti-CD20 mAbs) in multiple sclerosis (MS) has prompted increasing interest in treatment discontinuation and de-escalation strategies. In this perspective, we critically examine current data on outcomes following anti-CD20 discontinuation, including evidence from registries, prospective cohorts, and real-world studies. Available findings suggest that disease control achieved under anti-CD20 therapy is pharmacologically maintained rather than biologically resolved, and that B-cell repopulation following treatment cessation is heterogeneous and not reliably predictive of clinical stability. Reports of disease reactivation after discontinuation and the absence of validated biomarkers to identify patients who may safely stop therapy highlight substantial uncertainty. Current evidence therefore remains insufficient to support routine anti-CD20 discontinuation in MS, while a cautious, individualized approach-potentially incorporating dose-spacing strategies-may better reflect the current state of knowledge.

title: Longitudinal analysis of the effects of cladribine tablets on B and T cell memory recall responses to vaccine antigens in people with multiple sclerosis.
abstract: Cladribine tablets (CladT) are used as an immune reconstitution therapy for multiple sclerosis (MS). Patients are dosed in year 1 (time 0) and again after 12 months. The aim of therapy is to allow development of a reconstituted immune repertoire with reduced pathogenic autoreactivity. However, CladT could also affect the durability of memory T and antibody responses to bacterial and viral pathogens against which people with MS have previously been vaccinated. The objective of this study was to investigate changes in memory recall responses to vaccines over a 2-year period after the initial administration of CladT. Blood was collected prior to the initial administration of CladT and at 5 timepoints (3, 6, 12, 18 and 24 months) after administration from 18 people with MS. The effects of CladT on antigen-specific T cell and/or antibody responses to influenza, varicella zoster, tetanus toxoid, and SARS-CoV-2 were assessed. While levels of antibodies remained relatively stable for most vaccine antigens, numbers of T cells specific for the vaccine antigens declined in most individuals, particularly after the second course of treatment. Observations from individuals revaccinated against influenza suggest that revaccination at 18-24 months after starting CladT treatment, after both courses have been given, can restore influenza-specific responses. CladT treatment can cause a decline in numbers of vaccine-specific memory T cells. Numbers of influenza-specific memory T cells could be restored to pre-treatment levels by revaccination after the second course of treatment. Larger studies are needed to define antigen-specific revaccination schedules more broadly.

title: Zinc Supplementation Attenuates Pro-Inflammatory Cytokine Responses in a Cuprizone-Induced Rat Model of Multiple Sclerosis.
abstract: Multiple Sclerosis (MS) is a chronic autoimmune disorder marked by neuroinflammation, demyelination, and neurodegeneration. Zinc is crucial for immune regulation, but its impact on inflammatory cytokines in MS is not well understood. This study examined how dietary zinc status influences pro-inflammatory cytokine release in spinal cord tissue using a cuprizone-induced rat model of MS. The experimental cohort comprised 46 adult male Wistar rats, randomly allocated into five groups: Control (n=6) and four experimental groups "G" (n=10 each). G1 served as the untreated Control. G2, Sham-MS received daily oral gavage of carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC) solution-used as the vehicle for cuprizone-administered at 1% of their daily feed intake for 8 weeks. G3, G4, and G5 underwent MS induction via daily gavage of cuprizone dissolved in CMC at 1% of daily feed intake over the same period. G4 was maintained on a zinc-deficient diet (50 µg/kg zinc), whereas G5 received intraperitoneal zinc sulfate supplementation at 5 mg/kg/day. Disease progression was assessed by Rotarod performance and Myelin Basic Protein gene expression. Spinal cord levels of TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6 were measured by ELISA. Multiple sclerosis induction significantly increased TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6 levels (p <0.05), especially in zinc-deficient rats. Zinc supplementation attenuated these cytokine elevations, normalizing them to control levels (p <0.05). Functional and molecular data confirmed reduced disease severity with zinc repletion. Our findings reveal that zinc status is a critical modulator of neuroinflammation in an experimental MS model. Inflammatory cytokine levels in the spinal cord were significantly higher in both MS and zinc-deficient MS groups, confirming local inflammation associated with demyelination. Furthermore, zinc supplementation demonstrated a regulatory effect by suppressing the increase in inflammatory cytokines in the experimental MS model. These results may point to the therapeutic potential of zinc in MS management.

title: Predictors of Long-Term Disability in Multiple Sclerosis: Up to 10 Years of Follow-up in a Real-World Cohort Study.
abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) shows substantial interindividual variability in clinical course, yet early predictors of long-term disability remain incompletely defined. This retrospective cohort study aimed to investigate the impact of demographic characteristics, family history, comorbidities, and initial clinical and radiological features on disability progression over time. We retrospectively evaluated MS patients with respect to initial clinical presentation, relapse frequency, baseline magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) characteristics, early radiological progression, and acute relapse treatment. We also examined the association between recovery after the first relapse and long-term disability outcomes, assessed at years 1, 2, 5, and 10. Of the 346 patients, 69% were female, and the mean age was 43.4±11.0 years. Most patients had relapsing-onset disease (96%). Sensory symptoms and optic neuritis were the most common presenting symptoms, while motor and cerebellar onset were significantly associated with higher EDSS scores at years 1, 2, and 5. Relapse activity within the first year after diagnosis correlated positively with fifth-year EDSS, whereas relapse frequency prior to diagnosis showed no association with long-term progression. Neither the presence nor the number of contrast-enhancing MRI lesions predicted disability progression. Early clinical phenotype and early treatment response carry important prognostic information in MS. Motor or cerebellar onset, incomplete early recovery, and persistent relapse activity after diagnosis identify patients at higher risk for disability accumulation. Spinal cord involvement was the only MRI parameter associated with 10-year EDSS.

title: Familial Aggregation Patterns in Multiple Sclerosis and Their Association with Disease Severity.
abstract: Familial aggregation is a well-recognized feature of multiple sclerosis (MS). However, there is considerable heterogeneity in how disease susceptibility and clinical outcomes cluster within families. Although the relationship between parental lineage effects and MS risk has been previously investigated, their association with long-term disease severity remains poorly understood. In this study, we sought to explore patterns of familial aggregation according to maternal and paternal lineage in patients with familial MS and to evaluate whether these patterns are associated with long-term disease severity. This retrospective observational study included 110 patients with familial MS from 50 families. Among patients in whom parental lineage could be determined, familial aggregation was classified as maternal or paternal based on comprehensive pedigree review. Clinical characteristics, disability status measured by the Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS), and time-adjusted disease severity assessed using the Multiple Sclerosis Severity Score (MSSS) were compared between lineages. Maternal and paternal lineages differed significantly in the distribution of affected relatives by degree of relatedness (p=0.040); this difference was primarily driven by a higher proportion of first-degree affected relatives in the maternal-line group. No significant differences were observed between maternal and paternal lineages in early clinical characteristics, including age at onset, sex distribution, and initial clinical symptom distribution. Although EDSS scores were comparable between groups, MSSS values were significantly higher among patients in the maternal-line group (median 4.5 vs. 1.6, p=0.016). The parental lineage through which familial aggregation occurs in MS may be associated with long-term disease severity. These findings suggest that lineage-based approaches may offer valuable insights into the clinical profile of familial MS, while also underscoring the need for further studies integrating genetic, epigenetic, and longitudinal data.

title: Neuroinflammation in Alzheimer's disease: pathogenic signaling, biomarkers, and emerging therapeutic interventions.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the leading cause of dementia worldwide, characterized by progressive cognitive decline and neurodegeneration. Although amyloid-β plaques and hyperphosphorylated tau are major pathological hallmarks, increasing evidence highlights persistent neuroinflammation as a critical contributor to disease progression. Activated microglia and astrocytes, inflammatory cytokines, inflammasome activation, and dysregulated immune responses promote neuronal damage and synaptic dysfunction. Similar inflammatory mechanisms are observed in neurological disorders such as multiple sclerosis (MS) and brain tumors, suggesting shared molecular pathways linking neuroinflammation, neurodegeneration, and tumor-associated immune responses. Proteomics, transcriptomics, and multi-omics approaches provide powerful strategies to characterize disease-associated molecular signatures, signaling pathways, biomarkers, and therapeutic targets. This review summarizes key neuroinflammatory mechanisms in AD, including NF-κB, NLRP3, PI3K/Akt, MAPK, cGAS-STING, mitochondrial, lysosomal, calcium, insulin, and blood-brain barrier pathways. Recent advances in proteomic and transcriptomic profiling and their integration with genomic, epigenomic, and metabolomic data are discussed for understanding disease heterogeneity and identifying clinically relevant biomarkers. Current and emerging therapeutic strategies, including anti-Aβ antibodies, anti-inflammatory agents, selective inhibitors, dual-target compounds, PROTACs, and protein-protein interaction modulators, are also evaluated. Finally, multi-omics-based precision medicine and artificial intelligence-assisted analysis may facilitate biomarker-guided patient stratification and development of effective disease-modifying therapies.

title: Faecalibacterium prausnitzii in neurological disorders: mechanistic links and therapeutic potential along the microbiota-gut-brain axis.
abstract: Widespread dysbiosis in neurological disorders highlights the critical role of the microbiota-gut-brain axis (MGBA) and the therapeutic potential of probiotics in modulating the central nervous system (CNS).
